# Preface.

I have striven, in the biographies <note>The German term *Lebensbeschreibungen* literally means "descriptions of life."</note> which I now present to the public, to explain the history of the men I have depicted through the history of their time, and this in turn through the former; which method I shall also observe in the following essays. A series of selected biographies of famous scholars from the times of the <term>Restoration of the Sciences</term> <note>A common 18th-century term for the Renaissance, focusing on the "restoration" of Greek and Latin learning.</note> will perhaps teach us to know the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries better than a <term>pragmatic history</term> <note>In the 18th century, "pragmatic history" referred to a style of historical writing that focused on cause and effect, aiming to provide practical lessons for the reader rather than just a list of dates.</note> of the re-enlightenment of our Europe, because in such a history, one could not go into such precise detail as one can, and is permitted to do, in biographies. Moreover, a pragmatic history of the restoration of the sciences is infinitely difficult, because even the largest libraries never possess all the works of those men whose writings contain important data for the state of enlightenment in their

<summary>In this preface, Meiners argues that individual biographies offer a more detailed and effective way to understand the Renaissance (14th–16th centuries) than general historical surveys. He highlights the difficulty of writing comprehensive histories due to the scarcity of primary sources even in the largest libraries.</summary>
<keywords>biographical method, historiography, Renaissance, Restoration of the Sciences, Enlightenment, 18th-century scholarship, Christoph Meiners</keywords>

Historical or biographical fragments from the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth centuries are now extraordinarily interesting, both because of the striking similarities and the even greater differences between those centuries and our own. This first volume will be followed by a second, and perhaps even a third. I may break off wherever I wish, for I will certainly leave my successors much more material than I have the time or patience to process.

->Göttingen, July 25, 1794.<-

# Johann of Ravenna.

If any among the so-called <term>restorers of the sciences</term> <note>original: *Wiederherstellern der Wissenschaften*; this refers to the Humanists of the Renaissance who "restored" classical Latin and Greek learning after the Middle Ages.</note> from the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries deserves to have his memory renewed, and his venerable name rescued from oblivion, it is certainly Johann of Ravenna <note>Known in historical circles as Giovanni di Conversino da Ravenna (1343–1408), a key figure in the transition from the world of Petrarch to the early 15th-century humanists.</note>, the most beloved and meritorious pupil of Petrarch <note>original: *Petrarcha*; the 14th-century Italian poet and scholar considered the founder of Humanism.</note>. Johann of Ravenna taught just as excellently, and with such widespread benefit, as Petrarch had written; and through the oral instruction which he gave in the most prominent cities of Italy, he continued—with equal success and blessing—the great revolution in the manner of teaching and learning that Petrarch had begun through his example and his writings. Johann of Ravenna instructed all the immortal men who, at the beginning of the fifteenth century, pulled the works of Roman antiquity from the dust in which they lay buried in all the countries of Europe, and spread the new and better knowledge they contained throughout all Italy. He formed not only the mind, but also the heart of his listeners; and through his, and

<meta>This page continues the biography of Johann of Ravenna, specifically arguing for his pivotal role as a bridge between the initial spark of Petrarch and the later arrival of Greek scholars like Manuel Chrysoloras. It transitions from a general assessment of his historical importance to the specific details of his early life and education.</meta>

his most worthy pupils' character and life gave to the sciences he taught, and to the authors he interpreted, a reputation that the friends of the **old darkness** <note>The author uses "old darkness" to describe the Scholastic period or "Dark Ages," which the Humanists believed they were ending.</note> could no longer overcome. Without him, the light which Petrarch <note>Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the famous Italian poet and scholar.</note> had lit would likely have been, if not extinguished, at least obscured; and without the men whom he had made acquainted with the treasures of Roman literature and filled with an unquenchable thirst for Greek wisdom, Manuel Chrysoloras <note>A Byzantine scholar who was instrumental in reintroducing Greek literature to Western Europe.</note> would certainly not have been called to Italy, and the Greek language and literature would not have been awakened so soon. Johann of Ravenna was the **main link** in the chain by which, toward the end of the fourteenth century, the study of Roman and Greek literature was joined together. Providence sent him as a forerunner of Chrysoloras, tasked with clearing the path for him; and for this very reason, it was so arranged that these two great and remarkably similar men should meet not only in the same age but also in the same city, and were bound to share common pupils. Because, however, Johann of Ravenna only taught and did not write, and his memory survived only in the works of his teacher, his patrons, and his grateful pupils, his fame began to weaken soon after his death and finally disappeared so completely that his name was either entirely omitted by learned researchers of fourteenth and fifteenth-century history or was mentioned only briefly and in a manner not suited to his greatness. Mehus <note>Lorenzo Mehus (1717–1791), an Italian scholar and biographer who rediscovered many humanist texts.</note> was the first who, as it were, found the almost forgotten name of Johann of Ravenna again in the monuments of the past, and

said much to his just fame \*). As valuable as these reports are, they are neither entirely correct nor, much less, satisfactory; and Johann of Ravenna is worthy of having his fate, his character, and his merits depicted as in-depth as the few sources from which one can draw allow. Petrarch's letters are particularly rich regarding the early life of Johann of Ravenna; I will therefore translate them literally or provide a complete excerpt from them, because they paint the genius and temperament of the teacher and the pupil, as well as the times in which both lived, in a most interesting way and with the most vivid colors.

Johann Malpaghino, usually called Johann of Ravenna after his birthplace, was born in the year 1352 from a family that was neither wealthy nor noble \*\*). Nevertheless, his father sent him to the grammarian Donatus, a close friend of Petrarch, who at that time was teaching the Latin language in Venice with great acclaim. Donatus believed he discovered so many fortunate talents in the young Malpaghino that he recommended him to Petrarch not only as a faithful assistant for reading aloud, dictating, and transcribing, but also as a developing youth who was worthy of being educated by the greatest scholar of the fourteenth century. Johann of Ravenna fulfilled, and even exceeded, the hopes—

...feelings which his first teacher had stirred in him; and Petrarch soon loved and treated his new pupil as his own biological son. "One year after your departure," Petrarch writes to Giovanni of Certaldo <note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous author of the Decameron and Petrarch’s close friend, who lived in Certaldo.</note> \*), "I have received an excellent youth, whom I regret you do not know personally, and with whom I therefore wish to make you acquainted as far as can be done in a letter. He was born on the shores of the Adriatic Sea around the time when you lived in that city with the grandfather of the current Lord of Ravenna. His ancestry and financial circumstances are but modest. However, he possesses a moderation and a seriousness that would be praiseworthy even in an old man; and besides these virtues, a penetrating intellect, and a memory as quick to grasp as it is extensive and tenacious. My bucolic poem, which, as you know, consists of twelve eclogues <note>The *Bucolicum carmen*, a series of pastoral poems Petrarch wrote in imitation of Virgil.</note>, he learned by heart in twelve days; so that he recited one to me every evening, and on the last evening two eclogues without stumbling, as if he had the written poem itself before him. He himself possesses—what is very rare in our times—much poetic spirit, and a noble zeal for all beautiful and useful knowledge. His genius is a friend to the Muses, and he is already attempting his own poems, from which one can predict: That if the youth remains alive and continues in goodness as he has so far, something great will certainly come of him. Already much can be said of him. Thus far you have heard of only one part, namely his head, or his abilities. Now hear also of the best foundation of true wisdom and virtue."

Common people love money, and do not strive for it as much as he despises it and thrusts it away. It is in vain to try to force money upon him. He accepts barely as much as is required for a meager life. He competes with me in fasting, vigils <note>Periods of staying awake for prayer or study.</note>, and the love of solitude; and often he surpasses me. Through this conduct, he has become as dear to me as if he were my son; and perhaps even dearer than a biological son would be, because the latter, after the fashion of our young people, would want to dictate laws to his father, whereas the former does not follow his own will but my wishes—and indeed without any selfish intentions, purely out of love for me, and perhaps also in the hope of becoming better through my company. He came to me two years ago, and would to God that he had come sooner; though on account of his tender age he could not have come much earlier. He alone has successfully brought to order the collection of my letters, which I had almost entirely given up on because of their scattered state, and which four of my friends had tried in vain to complete; and a copy of them you will, I hope, soon receive, written by his own hand—not in such large and ostentatious letters as those with which the scribes, or rather the painters of our time, seek to flatter the eyes while actually tiring them out, but with a correct, legible, and pleasing script, in which neither the reader nor the grammarian will find anything to criticize \*). So that

...but I shall close with what I actually intended to begin with: the youth has a great inclination for <term>poetry<note>Original: *Dichtkunst*. In the Renaissance, this referred not just to rhyming, but to the entire art of classical composition and literature.</note></term>, in which he will one day—once he settles upon a certain direction—awaken joy and admiration in you. At present, due to the weakness of his age, he is still too wavering and, as it were, stumbling. He still thinks too little about what he wishes to say, and expresses what he does say with much pomp and ornament. Occasionally, he already produces a poem that unites harmony, beauty, and dignity within itself, and which anyone who did not know the author would attribute to an experienced and educated man. His mind and style will, I hope, gradually gain more firmness, and he will—I will not say flee—but rather so conceal the imitation of individual men that he seems like none of them, and will enrich the Latin language and poetry with a new style. At present, as his age naturally brings with it, he delights too much in the imitation of others; and, carried away by the beauty of ancient poems, he climbs so high against the laws of art that even when he notices it himself, or is made aware of it by others, he can only return with great difficulty. He admires <term>Virgil<note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro (70–19 BC), author of the *Aeneid*, who was the ultimate model for Renaissance Latin poets.</note></term> most of all, from whom he often inserts fragments into his own verses. As I watch him grow under my tutelage with heartfelt pleasure, and wish with all my heart that he may become what I myself would like to be, I warn him fatherly; I represent to him that what he writes must indeed be similar to his model, but not identical; similar in the way a son is to his father,

not as a portrait is to its original. A portrait is the better the more exactly it resembles the model. A son, on the other hand, can be unlike the father in almost every individual feature, and yet have a certain "air" by which everyone immediately recognizes the father \*). Just as the bees extract the nectar of the flowers without retaining their color, and prepare from various juices a honey that is better than any single juice from which it was made; so must poets and writers indeed appropriate the thoughts of others, and even their "colors," but never speak with their words. When I recently repeated these warnings, he answered me: "I confess that you are right; but many examples, and even your own, have prompted me to use successful turns of phrase and expressions from great writers now and then." To this I replied, full of wonder: "If you ever encounter such things in my writings, know that this happened not intentionally, but through an oversight. Notwithstanding that such examples frequently occur in good writers, I nevertheless strive with all my might—and herein lies one of the greatest difficulties in writing for me—to tread neither in the footsteps of others, nor in my own. Meanwhile, I should like to know what example you have found in my writings?" "In your sixth <term>Eclogue<note>A pastoral poem. Petrarch's *Bucolicum carmen* contained twelve such poems.</note></term>," he said, "a verse ends with the words: *And he thunders with his voice* <note>original: "Atque intonat ore." This is a phrase from Virgil's *Aeneid* (Book XII, 307).</note>." As soon as I heard the words, I also noticed that they were the ending of a Virgilian verse. I report this to you so that you may reproach yourself for not having shown me my oversight.

Not long after Petrarch had sent this letter of praise for his young friend, the youth was seized by an irresistible desire to see the world. All the arguments that the distressed Petrarch made to the enthusiastic youth regarding the recklessness and danger of his decision were in vain. It is impossible to describe the struggle between the benefactor and teacher and the straying, headstrong pupil—the paternal indulgence and the paternal indignation of Petrarch, and the steadfastness of the young Malpaghini—more movingly or attractively than Petrarch himself did in a letter to the grammarian <term>Donatus<note>Donato degli Albanzani (c. 1326–1411), a famous grammarian and close friend of Petrarch.</note></term> *). Neither from this nor from the following letters can one precisely determine the time when Johann of Ravenna came to his second teacher, or when he left him for the first time. It is probable that the young Malpaghini was only fourteen, at most fifteen years old, when he was first taken in by Petrarch; thus, his first departure from this great teacher occurred at the beginning of the seventeenth or eighteenth year of our Johann of Ravenna’s life.

"Among the greatest unpleasantnesses of my life," Petrarch writes to Donatus, "I count those which I experienced yesterday. That very youth, whom you formerly, and I afterward, had adopted as a son; with whose praise I filled the ears

This youth, the joy and comfort of us both, came to me yesterday evening with a countenance and heart quite different from what I had previously observed in him, and declared that he could no longer stay with me, but wished to depart immediately. These expressions struck, or rather shook me so greatly, that I threw away my pen, paper, and all the thoughts with which I was just then occupied, and for a long time observed the young man in silence, full of the most heartfelt pity for the inconstancy of his age. Since I believed I had read his sentiments sufficiently from his face, I asked him quite calmly whether I, or one of my friends,

He denied this and added that he knew very well that he would nowhere find such a peaceful and honorable residence again. As he said this, he burst into tears, which seemed sincere to me because just a few days earlier, among other writings he brought me, I had found a draft—written in his own hand—of a short letter to a friend. In it, he replied to the friend's encouragement to leave me: the plan the friend had suggested was not good advice; he, my <term>protégé<note>The German "Zögling" implies a student who is being raised or mentored under a guardian's care.</note></term>, lived in the most perfect peace of soul, and he had found not merely a master and benefactor, but a father. Upon comparing the contents of this letter with his present declarations, my pity and my wonder increased in equal measure. "Unhappy youth!" I cried out, "if it is as you say; if you lack nothing you desire, and if nothing has happened to offend you, what then hunts you, or where are you throwing yourself?" "Nothing," he replied, amid increasingly heavy tears, "except that I can no longer write." Here I could not restrain myself from laughing out of indignation and asking him: "Are your hands then trembling, or have your eyes grown weak?" — "Neither," he replied. "But the zeal for writing has not only grown cold, it has vanished entirely, and I can in no way be persuaded again to copy books or manuscripts." — "Then what has happened to you," I said, "is what you deserved. Did I not often warn you not to write so persistently? Now, excess in this labor has, as usual, produced disgust and satiety. Therefore, stop writing for a

while. Do as wise country-folk do, who let the exhausted field rest for a half or a whole year; and you will find the <term>proverb of the ancients<note>Likely a reference to the Ovidian sentiment that "Time heals all wounds," or similar classical adages about the restorative power of rest.</note></term> to be true: that time may wound, but it also heals. Your malady will be best remedied by variety. Think about and do something else for a while. New tasks will give you a desire for the old ones again." — When I had brought this forward and wanted to add similar things, he interrupted me and protested, half sadly and half indignantly: "That he would never write again, neither for me nor for any other person." "Very well," I replied: "Even if you no longer wish to do that, why should we part because of it? I have held you not as my <term>scribe<note>Petrarch relied heavily on scribes to copy his works and classical manuscripts, as this was the only way to "publish" or preserve books before the invention of the printing press.</note></term>, but as my son. If you no longer wish to write, you can instead read aloud, converse with me, or accompany me; you can adorn this little house, which perhaps in turn will adorn you and make you worthy of a better dwelling." — "Even this does not stop me," the youth answered. "I do not wish to live anywhere where I can be of no use. I feel my worth too much to want to eat unearned bread. My firm intention is to go. I beg you to release me, for otherwise I shall tear myself away, even against your will." These words provoked me more violently. "Miserable one," I said, "do you despise yourself so much as to believe that if you are not a scribe, you are then nothing? Truly, you had raised greater expectations of yourself. Your legible, neat <term>handwriting<note>Petrarch was a famous advocate for "humanist minuscule," a clear and elegant script that eventually became the basis for modern Roman typefaces. He despised the messy, cramped "Gothic" scripts used by medieval legal scholars.</note></term>, so different from the usual dazzling style, I did not take to be a fruit of your genius, but rather the bloom or the prelude to a future scholarship of no common sort. I do not know, the noble Petrarch continues, whether it would not have been more modest to have left the latter unsaid. However, pain and anger often lead one to a certain boastfulness, into which one would never have fallen through vanity or pride. 

Upon this, I reminded him of the words of his Bishop: that he, as a young man, might perhaps live in greater abundance in another house, but nowhere more honorably, nor with more benefit for his future, than in mine. He should consider maturely whether my company, for as long as we have lived together, did not seem tolerable enough to him—and after my death, glorious enough—if indeed he should outlive me, which his youth promises more than the current weakness of his body. It could hardly bring him shame to have been my confidant, my friend, my self-chosen son, and the heir to my name, however meager that name may be. — “All in vain!” he finally cried; “you will not catch me with such snares.” After he had said this, he ran away, and went straight

I begged him to tell me the true cause of his departure; I told him I would then not only release him with good will, but also provide him with powerful letters of recommendation to my friends in the regions where he intended to go, along with the necessary travel money. His likely false pretense offended me more than his leaving. He persisted, however, in his first statement, and swore holily that he had no other reason to part from me than the one he had brought forward. Nevertheless, I and several of my friends cannot believe otherwise than that he is drawn elsewhere by the hope of greater advantages, or is truly being driven about by madness. I do not know which of these cases is the true one; but both have much probability. Because of the praises I gave him, he had begun to please many, and this praise and applause could have initially produced in him a great opinion of himself, and later easily a confusion of the mind. I am not the only one who has noticed that the young man's eyes have, for some time now, been more watery and more wandering than usual. ---

In the entire series of scenes which **Petrarcha** has depicted in the letter shared here, this wise man appears infinitely more amiable and venerable than the young **John of Ravenna**. No father could have listened more indulgently, warned more well-meaningly, instructed more concisely, or called back more kindly to his most beloved son—after such an unexpected and undeserved declaration as the youth made to his teacher—than **Petrarcha** listened to, warned, instructed, and called back **John of Ravenna**. However, **Petrarcha** erred in his judgment, if not of the youth’s character, then at least of his mental state; the hot-headed youth did not know himself or what was happening within him, and for that very reason, he led his teacher toward incorrect assumptions, appearing much more blameworthy than he actually was.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Petrarch’s relationship with his young secretary, Giovanni Malpaghini (also known as John of Ravenna). Nothing was more natural than that a life so quiet and uniform, such as the young Malpaghino lived with Petrarch, would gradually stir up weariness and satiety in a fiery youth, and produce a hot longing for a change in his condition—especially for a completely opposite situation, which must have appeared all the more enchanting to him the more repulsive his previous state became. But since the well-meaning and grateful youth deeply loved and revered his benefactor; since he lacked nothing in his house, and nothing happened to him about which he could have complained—so he suppressed for a time the wish to leave Petrarch, and even resisted the promptings of friends who sought to persuade him to do so. 

Despite all these efforts, the suppressed desire broke forth again and again. The struggle between this desire and what he believed he owed to himself and to Petrarch became more and more violent, and manifested itself through restless and wild looks, in which signs of madness were later found. Finally, the longing for a new way of being triumphed over everything by which he had previously kept it in check; and in the moment of such a victory of passion, he went to Petrarch to make known the resolution he had made. 

Even the dryness and defiance with which John of Ravenna announced to his teacher that he wished to leave him are, in my eyes, no evidence of insensitivity or ingratitude, but rather of anxiety regarding the reproaches and difficulties his teacher would present to him. At the first questions Petrarch put to him, the youth dissolved into tears and sincerely confessed that he had lacked nothing until then, and also that nothing unpleasant...

<page-num>21</page-num>

...had happened to him. Since John of Ravenna did not recognize the true cause of his unrest and dissatisfaction, in justifying his resolution, he fell upon the most important service he had rendered Petrarch until then, and which might have become burdensome to him at times due to the excessive zeal with which he had performed it, regardless of the warnings of his benefactor. 

A dim feeling told the impatient youth that if he expressed his dislike for this work performed until then <note>This "work" refers to the laborious task of transcribing Petrarch's messy drafts into clean, calligraphic copies—a job for which Giovanni was exceptionally gifted.</note>, Petrarch would be all the more likely to dismiss him as a useless person. If the wish to separate from Petrarch had arisen solely from a disgust for <term>copying</term> <note>original: "Abschreiben"; the manual reproduction of manuscripts before the invention of the printing press.</note>, then the kindness with which his benefactor freed him from this work would have calmed the mind of John of Ravenna at once and reconciled him with his previous situation. 

Even this release from a meritorious task produced not the slightest change in the young man's resolution, because this work was by no means the only thing that had brought about the decision. Meanwhile, John of Ravenna did not know how to ward off the fatherly offer of his benefactor other than by saying: He would and could no longer stay in a house where he was no longer useful. If he had not expected that Petrarch would release him entirely from the copying, he certainly expected even less that his foster father would answer him with wise indulgence: He, Petrarch, had hitherto regarded his pupil not as a servant, but as a son; and this son should not despise himself so much as to believe that if he no longer copied for his foster father, he could then no longer be useful to him. By this rebuttal, John of Ravenna was completely disarmed, but not convinced, and still less won over. Rather, the young man was embittered by the shame he felt through the refutation of all the reasons he had put forward; and in this bitterness, he answered the question of what he intended to say to his teacher Donatus <note>Donato degli Albanzani, a grammarian and a close friend of Petrarch who had previously taught Giovanni.</note> with these harsh words: "What have I to do with Donatus?" Petrarch was rightly incensed by these seemingly ungrateful words; and yet, if one places oneself in the youth's position and interprets the answer according to all his subsequent behavior, they were not so much the effect of a complete forgetfulness of what he owed to his first teacher, as they were shame over the inability to bring forward anything better, and resentment over the danger that his favorite plan might be thwarted by irresistible kindness and irrefutable reasons. Now, all other representations and signs of paternal condescension and mildness were of no further use. John of Ravenna remained firm in his resolution and took a sudden leave of Petrarch, as if he feared that he would not be able to resist him in the long run. Since Petrarch did not suspect the true cause of the persistence in a purpose that seemed highly groundless and dangerous, he necessarily had to assume that the young man was either concealing the true reasons for his decision or that he was not quite in his right mind. Based on the first of these assumptions, it can be explained how Petrarch could mock the future great works of the youth, whom he considered proud and conceited. In either assumption, however, it would have been more worthy of Petrarch's wisdom and goodness if he had not regarded it as something amusing

<column-break/>

<page-num>23</page-num>

that the young Malpaghini <note>Giovanni Malpaghini (c. 1346–1417), Petrarch's secretary, who later became a famous scholar in his own right.</note> had brought upon himself the reputation of madness through his over-hasty and misunderstood behavior. This rumor harmed the young man, and not only could it not cure him of his passion or mental distress, but it rather had to worsen it and strengthen him in the thought of leaving a city as soon as possible where he had been done the greatest injustice and where people had begun to doubt his sanity.

The outcome proved the truth of this observation. John of Ravenna allowed nothing more to stop him and left Padua without recommendations, without companions, and without travel money. Petrarch describes the departure of his pupil, his travels, fates, and return, in the very next letter to Donatus, in the following manner <margin>*) Book V, Letter 7.</margin>.

> "The young person was held back for a short time, partly by my persuasion and partly by the outcry of others. Soon, however, it became clear what he was plotting. His body was constantly in motion; his soul was even more restless, and one might almost say, was everywhere at once. Now he wanted to go to Naples, now to Calabria, or the birthplace of Ennius <note>The ancient poet Ennius was born in Rudiae, near modern Lecce.</note>, or even to Constantinople. It is almost unbelievable that a young person who had grown up until now under the rod, who possesses neither wealth nor health, has suddenly reached such a level of boldness and stubbornness that with the very ears that only yesterday feared your voice and that of your assistant, and the disciplinary rod, today he defies yours, mine, and all our..."

...rejects the warnings of friends, and no longer cites his dislike of transcribing and similar tasks as the cause of his wild undertaking—as he did at first—but now alleges a violent desire for the Greek language and literature. When I pointed out to him how much he still lacked in a perfect knowledge of the Latin language; when I coupled this with his poverty, his weak health, the dangers and hardships of travel, the desolation of Greece, and the ignorance of the modern Greeks <note>During the 14th century, many Western scholars like Petrarch idealized Ancient Greece but viewed the contemporary Byzantine Greeks with skepticism or disdain.</note>; he nevertheless stubbornly resisted all these warnings. He was driven by secret motives which he carefully concealed until the very end, using his love for new and useful knowledge as a pretext. I shall remain silent about these secret driving forces, lest it seem as though I am more angry about youthful errors than I ought to be.

The first and strongest among all these motives is an inconstancy <note>Petrarch often complained of the "fickleness" (inconstantia) of youth, a common theme in his moral philosophy.</note> which has perhaps made a different impression on others, but on me it has made such an impression that I must confess: I have never heard nor read of such flightiness and instability, much less experienced a similar case myself. At one and the same time, the young man revolves so many and such contradictory things in his little mind, as if he had a thousand souls at war with one another; he is so unlike himself from one hour to the next that nothing is constant in him but his own changeability. The end of all these conflicting thoughts was that he wished to visit the **Babylon of the West** <note>original: "Babylon des Abendlandes"; Petrarch’s famous epithet for Avignon, the seat of the Papal Court, which he considered a place of corruption and exile.</note>. No sooner thought than done. He ran away without taking the letters of recommendation I wished to give him for my friends, in which I had recommended his foolish resolution as a drive for higher things. *Nature* soon punished the obstinacy of the vagabond.

<column-break/>

<page-num>25</page-num>

He crossed the Apennines under constant downpours and pretended to every acquaintance he met that he had been sent by me; for he soon began to wake from his dream and feel the shame that awaits a wanderer. By pretending to be on a mission from me, he aroused in several persons—as I later learned—an undeserved pity and, at the same time, disadvantageous suspicions against me: that I would send such a weak and inexperienced youth away without company or proper support.

Finally, he came to Pisa and the Tyrrhenian Sea to take ship there. But as he found no ship for some time, and his impatience grew just as much as his money melted away, he suddenly resolved to go back over the Apennines. He knows best the hardships and dangers with which he made this journey. One can easily imagine that a weak young man, who knew neither the roads nor the people and was incessantly soaked by heavy rains, suffered a great deal on the rocky heights and in the deep valleys of the Apennines, through which swollen mountain streams flowed.

When he finally descended into the Ligurian plain and tried to wade through the Farma river in the Parmesan territory, he fell into a whirlpool that would have eventually hurled him down to the underworld if someone had not come along and become his savior. After surviving this obvious mortal danger, he finally arrived here—emaciated by hunger, stripped of money, exhausted by the hardships of the journey, and filthy or ragged—where he knew I would be, or would soon arrive. When he first presented himself to my *Franciscus* <note>Likely referring to Petrarch's son-in-law, Francescuolo da Brossano, who managed the poet's household.</note>, the latter did not recognize him at first, as he did not look so much like a living being as a...

I know now how I must conduct myself with this fugitive; and if I did not know, your letters and advice would teach me. — In the meantime, you know that no wrong is so great that I cannot easily forget and forgive it; and no enemy so bitter that I could not pity and love him if he comes to me ashamed and repentant. My leniency may often be harmful to me, but it can never be detrimental to my good reputation. I would rather the guilt be entirely on his side than have ill-intentioned people attribute even a part of it to me; let them call him inconstant rather than call me harsh. If he ever fully comes to his senses again—which I doubt—he shall come to know himself, and me, and the advice of my friends which he despised; he shall punish himself through shame and repentance. Let him act according to his way, and I will act according to mine.”

->Written at Pavia in July.<-

<column-break/>

<page-num>27</page-num>

The distrust and the cooled affection with which Petrarch received the returning runaway were justified, just as the kindness with which he set aside the necessary funds for John of Ravenna, in case of a similar lapse, was highly noble. Petrarch erred only in writing this letter, as in the previous one, by labeling John of Ravenna’s urge to leave his teacher’s quiet home as "inconstancy," and by considering the youth the most fickle creature he had ever heard or read of. John of Ravenna was only too firm in his resolve to change his situation. Since he could no longer use his aversion to transcribing as the reason for his separation from Petrarch, he cited the desire to see the world or to learn the Greek language as causes. Both were not, as Petrarch suspected, mere pretexts, but true causes; and they were even less in conflict with one another. Petrarch became unjust not in his behavior, but in his judgment of John of Ravenna.

Through pleas, paternal warnings, and earnest reproaches, Petrarch kept the returned youth from further adventures for about a year. Then the old illness or mental unrest <note>A reference to the "restless spirit" or "accidie" often discussed in medieval psychology.</note> of the young Malpaghini broke out irresistibly once more; and now Petrarch gave the departing pupil the following letters of recommendation, which bring perhaps even more honor to his wisdom and good-naturedness than the letters I have already cited.

“The youth whom you see before you,” he writes to Hugo de St. Severino <margin>*) Book XI, *Rerum senilium* (Letters of Old Age), Letter 9. <note>original Latin: "Lib. XI. Rer. senil. Ep. 9."</note></margin> *), “was with me for several years...

[...] for years, like a son, and he does not stop being one even now. For although he separates himself from me physically, I hope that he will not do so in his heart. The step that leads him away from me I attribute not so much to him as to his age, which does not yet have enough stability and finds pleasure in wandering; a tendency that—lest I accuse only myself—accompanies many people even into their latest old age. This youth, among many plans that arose within him, has finally seized upon the noblest one, and since he wished to travel anyway, he has resolved to do so only with the intention of satisfying his curiosity. 

In particular, he has a violent thirst for the Greek language, and as a youth he nourishes a wish that Cato <note>Cato the Elder (234–149 BCE), a Roman statesman who famously did not begin to learn the Greek language until he was eighty years old.</note> only conceived in his old age. For a year, I have sought to restrain this wish with no small amount of art and labor; sometimes through pleas, sometimes through reproaches; sometimes by pointing out how much he still lacks in his knowledge of the Latin language <note>Original: "römischen Sprache" (Roman language).</note>; sometimes by explaining the hardships and dangers that would certainly befall him on such a journey, especially since he had already left once and was very quickly brought back to me by the distress into which he fell. 

As long as the memory of this unfortunate journey remained fresh, he stayed quiet and gave hope that his boisterous spirit could be tamed and guided. But now that time has gradually weakened the memory of the hardships he endured, he longs for the world again and can be restrained neither by force nor by persuasion. Driven by a curiosity more fiery than rational, he wishes to leave his fatherland, friends, relatives, his old father, and me, whom

Namely, he now wants to visit Calabria and the entire coast of Italy that was formerly called Great Greece <note>Original: "Großgriechenland," referring to *Magna Graecia*, the coastal areas of Southern Italy settled by Greeks in antiquity where the language and culture persisted longer than elsewhere in the West.</note>, because I told him a few times that in these regions some men very knowledgeable in the Greek language were found, especially a monk Barlaam and Leo or Leontius <note>Barlaam of Seminara and Leontius Pilatus were 14th-century scholars who were instrumental in reintroducing Greek literature to the Latin West. Because of this intention, he has asked me for a letter of recommendation to you, who are so influential everywhere, and especially in those regions. I did this because I hope that the young man can provide you with as much pleasure through his spirit and knowledge as you can provide him with benefit through your authority. I love the youth, and although I do not so much approve of as excuse the instability of his mind, I cannot blame his desire to learn. He is rather worthy of obtaining that which he so vehemently desires that he forgets not only all his previous connections and all difficulties, but even himself and his frail health. I therefore recommend him to you most earnestly; and if you assist him with counsel and deed, you will certainly perform a work pleasing to God, and [me]...

Petrarch gave his pupil, around that same time, a similar letter of recommendation addressed to Franciscus Brunus <note>Francesco Bruni (d. 1385), a close friend of Petrarch and a papal secretary.</note> in Rome. \*) "The person," Petrarch writes to the aforementioned friend, "from whose hands you will receive this letter, was with me for over three years, not as a member of the household, but as a son. I have held him as a father, warned him as a father, praised and rebuked him as a father, loved him as a father, and—to your surprise—I now hate him as a father. It is he of whom I reported to you long ago, that he writes so correctly, and by whose hand the letter was written which I, on your advice, addressed to the Pope, and which you yourself delivered. This young person came to me rich in gifts of the spirit, but poor in knowledge. Now I may boast, and refer to the testimony of the bearer himself, that although it was not through my formal instruction, but through my company and guidance, he leaves me more learned than he was when he came to me. I wished I could say that he left me upon my advice and with my free consent. But—he is a young person, and wants to try the world, as I once did myself, though I cannot look back on it without a shudder. \*\*) He wishes to see Rome; a wish I cannot disapprove of, since I have seen this city so often and would still gladly see it again. At the same time, however, I suspect that he wants to venture out onto an even larger sea, and his fortune

After this letter, **Johann von Ravenna** had wandered astray for a long time before he came to the unnamed patron, from whose house he wrote to **Petrarch** stating that he had found a permanent place. **Petrarch's** reply is written in a serious, almost unfriendly tone, which proves that his anger over the departure and this aimless wandering of **Johann von Ravenna** had diminished only slightly. On the other hand, **Petrarch** expressed himself quite differently when he mentioned his former pupil to persons who could advance his fortune. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Giovanni Malpaghini (Johann von Ravenna), following the account of his restless youth and his complex relationship with his mentor, Petrarch. <page-num>36</page-num>

...would the departed spirit of **Petrarch** rejoice—if indeed he could descend into his former earthly dwellings—to hear his most beloved pupil, of whose development he had at times begun to despair, not only teaching in Padua in a manner worthy of his great master, but also to see him living and acting so?

Already in Padua, **Johann von Ravenna** <note>Also known as Giovanni Malpaghini (c. 1346–1417), a key figure in the transition to Renaissance humanism.</note> was forming, if not the most numerous, then at least his greatest students, who became the primary causes of his fame as well as the remarkable revolution in scholarship that spread throughout all Italy at the beginning of the fifteenth century. Almost all of **Johann von Ravenna's** students who later became teachers or writers surpassed their master—not in virtue or spirit, but in erudition and the beauty of their Latin style. They were easily able to surpass him in this regard because many important works of Roman antiquity were only discovered in the final years of **Johann von Ravenna's** life, or even after his death. Nonetheless, all of **Johann von Ravenna's** students recognized that this teacher had been granted to them through a special divine providence, and that he had been the first teacher of the modern era to revive the study of the authentic Latin language and the works of Roman antiquity, making them universal in their fatherland. One should hear the testimony of **Blondus** <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a pioneering Renaissance historian and humanist.</note>, which is instructive in many respects.

<meta>This page continues the translated testimony of the historian Flavio Biondo regarding the legacy of Johann von Ravenna (Giovanni Malpaghini). It lists his most influential students and describes the transition into the "Age of Discovery" for classical manuscripts.</meta>

<page-num>38</page-num>

**Annebonus of Padua**, **Roberto de' Rossi**, **Jacopo Angeli of Florence**, **Poggius**, **Guarino of Verona**, **Vittorino**, **Sicco**, and other less famous men, whom he inflamed to the study of better knowledge and the imitation of **Cicero**, even if he could not perfectly train or instruct them himself. Around the same time, **Manuel Chrysoloras** <note>A pioneering teacher of Greek in the West (c. 1350–1415) who helped reintroduce Greek literature to Italy.</note> came from Constantinople to Italy—a man as virtuous as he was learned—and taught nearly all the aforementioned students of **Johann von Ravenna** the Greek language, partly in Venice and partly in Florence and Rome. After he had continued this instruction for several years, the opinion arose in Italy that he who did not know the Greek language and the ancient Greek writers was more ignorant than he who understood no Latin.

Suddenly, countless men and youths were seized by an enthusiasm for the works of Greek and Roman antiquity. When, therefore, the **Council of Constance** <note>Held from 1414 to 1418; while intended to settle church schisms, it served as a gathering point for humanists to hunt for manuscripts in nearby monasteries.</note> was held at the beginning of the fifteenth century, many of our people searched in this and neighboring cities and monasteries to see if they could find lost Roman manuscripts. **Poggius** <note>Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), a famous "manuscript hunter" and papal secretary.</note> first discovered a complete manuscript of **Quintilian** <note>The *Institutio Oratoria*, a foundational text on education and rhetoric.</note>, which was soon followed by **Cicero’s** *Letters to Atticus* <note>original: "Briefe des Cicero an den Atticus"</note>. As our youth studied these works with the greatest diligence, the famous grammarian and rhetorician **Gasparinus of Bergamo** opened a school in Venice that was much better than any previous ones, and in which young men were encouraged to study the ancient language and writers. Around the same time, **Petrus Paulus Vergerius**, **Leonardo Aretino**, **Roberto de' Rossi**, **Jacopo Angeli**, and **Pog-**

The ever-increasing study of ancient literature was extraordinarily promoted by the fact that Bishop **Gerardo Landriani** at Lodi found, among ruins, a very old codex of **Cicero** written in barely legible characters. Among other rhetorical writings of this great Roman, it contained the complete books *On the Orator* <note>original: "de oratore"</note>, the *Brutus*, and *The Orator* <note>original: "Orator"</note>. When I came to Milan in my youth on the business of my hometown, I was the first to transcribe **Cicero’s** *Brutus* with equal zeal and speed, and then sent copies of my transcription to **Guarino** in Verona and **Leonardo Giustiniani** in Venice; whereupon this work was soon spread throughout all of Italy. Through all these new works, eloquence received ever-new fuel, and thus it happened that in our age one speaks and writes better than in the age of **Petrarch**. <meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Italian humanism to the German context, specifically focusing on Johann Reuchlin. It serves as an introduction to a biography of Reuchlin and his pivotal role in the intellectual transition toward the Reformation.</meta>

<page-num>44</page-num>

# Short Biography of Reuchlin,
### Assessment of his character and his writings, and history of his conflict with the theologians in Cologne.

---

In the last twenty years of the fifteenth and the first of the sixteenth century, besides **Luther** and **Erasmus**, no other scholar gave such a push to his own and subsequent ages as **Reuchlin**, and indeed, not merely through his useful teachings and writings, but also through his errors. If I further except **Luther**, and in the latter years of the specified period also the great martyr of German freedom, **Ulrich von Hutten**; then among the scholars who flourished alongside **Reuchlin**, none could be found whose life shed so great a light on the history of the departing fifteenth and the beginning sixteenth century as that of **Reuchlin**. No other life allows one to so clearly recognize the condition of the schools and all sciences, the customs, and the almost unbelievable arrogance of the clergy, the beginning of the serious struggle between the new light and the old darkness, the beneficial influences of the increasingly revealing and spreading truth upon customs, and the final necessary preparations for the glorious **Reformation** <note>Reuchlin's work in Hebrew studies and his defense of Jewish books against the Inquisition are seen here as precursors to the Reformation’s spirit of inquiry.</note>, as does

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<page-num>45</page-num>

the life of **Reuchlin**. Reflective readers will surely be astonished that nearly one hundred and fifty years after the revival of Greek and Roman literature, and fifty years after the invention of the **printing press**, it was still so difficult to educate oneself by reading good books, as it truly was in the age of **Reuchlin**. It is astonishing that all schools and academic disciplines were still so completely corrupted at the beginning of the sixteenth century, especially in **Germany**; and yet no large European country had so many enlightened spiritual and secular princes and lords—or those favorable to enlightenment—nor so many famous teachers and writers as **Germany**. It is remarkable that many princes, cities, and cathedral chapters, a large part of the nobility, and all true friends of truth and virtue allied themselves with **Reuchlin**; and yet all these combined forces were not sufficient to win a decisive victory over a single **mendicant order** <term>Mendicant Order</term><note>The author refers here to the Dominicans of Cologne, who led the legal and theological assault against Reuchlin.</note>, even if they did make victory easier for the combatants who followed. Even the great differences, and again the striking similarities, of the Reuchlinian age with our own, impart a charm to the life of this wise man which has determined me to renew the memory of it just now, as I had long intended to do. All teachers and defenders of truth will draw manifold comfort from **Reuchlin’s** life; they will certainly wish that the **Estates** <term>Estates</term><note>The social and political ranks (nobility, clergy, etc.) that held power in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> which upheld **Reuchlin** might also stand by them now; but they will also not despair if they are forced to faithfully fulfill their duties solely under the shield of truth *).

---

*) Several writers have recounted the life and merits of **Reuchlin**. See **Burkhard** <note>original: "de fatis et meritis Ulrici"</note> *On the Fates and Merits of Ulrich*...

Johann Reuchlin was born in the year 1455 \*) in the city of Pforzheim to middle-class parents who were wealthy enough to send their sons to the Latin school in their town. Our Reuchlin distinguished himself from his fellow students through his diligence and his strong, beautiful voice. Because of the latter, toward the end of his seventeenth or the beginning of his eighteenth year, he was called to the court of Baden and admitted among the court singers, or the choir students, who

<margin>
The most prominent sources are Melanchthon in his speech *On the Life of Capnio* <note>Capnio is the Greek translation of Reuchlin's name, meaning "smoky."</note>, and Heinrich Majus in the *Life of Johann Reuchlin* (Durlach, 1687). Melanchthon's speech contains some otherwise unknown reports, but also several false ones, which I will note in the following. The biography by Majus is much more complete. However, even he did not carefully enough collect all the data from the writings of Reuchlin, his opponents, and his friends that would illuminate Reuchlin's character, merits, and errors—and even less so those details that shed light on the times in which this man lived. Majus did not know Reuchlin's era well enough, nor did he pay enough attention to the benefit and harm that Reuchlin brought about. Yet it is precisely the times in which Reuchlin lived, and the changes he brought about in them, for which his history is still so remarkable today. I will spend much less time on what one calls "life circumstances"; instead, I will expand upon Reuchlin's character, his merits and errors, the connections he held, and especially his conflict with the Dominican Order, in a more precise and, I hope, more instructive detail than my predecessor has done. Burkhard, in his book *On the Fates of the Latin Language in Germany* (Hanover, 1713), provides much on page 136 and following, but nothing new regarding Reuchlin.

In his twentieth year, Reuchlin turned toward **Basel**, where he was immediately granted a Master’s degree, and the **Amerbach brothers** <note>Famous early printers in Basel</note> commissioned him to produce a Latin dictionary, which he published under the title *Breviloquus* <note>Meaning "Short-speaker" or "Concise Dictionary"</note> \*\*). After he had enjoyed the instruction of Andronikus for about two years, he not only continued his study of Latin grammar and the Roman authors, but he also began—at the advice of Andronikus himself—to interpret Greek grammar and Greek authors in Basel \*). Reuchlin presented Latin and Greek grammar, as well as the writers of both languages, in such a way that his listeners were guided more toward correct reading and writing than toward a beautiful prose style, because the former was the most that could be achieved at that time \*\*). He taught in Basel with a fame and acclaim that no other teacher at this high school possessed, and he succeeded not only in being the first to awaken the study of ancient literature in Basel, but also in making it a dominant field of study among the youth residing there †).

Anno 1477. Basileae."</note> "Therefore, relying on your learning and our authority, you should instruct those wishing to hear Greek literature, so that they themselves may become more learned daily, and you yourself may be more clear and elegant in reading the authors. As soon as the youth found a taste for a better language, for better writers, and for a pure Aristotelian philosophy drawn from the original sources, they abandoned and despised the dry scholastic methods which had been thrust upon them until then. This necessarily provoked the teachers of the old philosophy and theology, who all cried out together that the Greeks were schismatics <note>Those who split from the Roman Catholic Church</note>; that their teachings had been forbidden by the Church, and that their literature conflicted with the true faith. Reuchlin remained in Linz until the death of Frederick III, which occurred in the autumn of 1493 \*). All Württemberg historians recount that Reuchlin was also among the glittering retinue of **Eberhard the Pious** when the latter traveled to the important Imperial Diet at Worms. It was there—with the consent of all the Estates of the Empire and to the most vivid joy of all good and noble men in all Germany—that Eberhard was elevated to become the first Duke of Württemberg \*\*). However, Reuchlin’s letters prove that he was not a witness to these festivities; instead, he was in Tübingen, waiting inconsolably and in vain for news of the events happening in Worms and Italy. Furthermore, they show that the new Duke was the first among absent friends to think of Reuchlin \*\*\*).

Around this time, Reuchlin had completed his work *De verbo mirifico* <note>original: "On the Miracle-Working Word," a foundational text of the Christian Kabbalah</note> and sent it to his friend and student, **Sebastian Brant**, in Basel, so that it might be printed in 그 city. Sebastian Brant deeply regretted that Reuchlin was so overwhelmed by all sorts of public and even military affairs that he had almost no time left for scholarly work. His only consolation was that Reuchlin was destined for higher things, and that he dedicated all his strength to the service of the best, most beloved, and most revered prince of his time †). Among these friends of **Dalberg**, it seems Reuchlin loved none so much, or at least lived with none so familiarly, as with his **Vigilius**; and it is indeed touching to read the description of the joyful and brotherly intimacy with which these two men in Heidelberg were sick together, slept together ††), and in the process of dressing, mixed up their linens or clothes. In the very first weeks or months of his stay in Heidelberg, Reuchlin, for the entertainment of his patron **von Dalberg**, composed a Latin comedy titled *Sergius*, which was intended to be performed by a few select students. In this comedy, Reuchlin presented a company of parasites and cheats, among whom one had the idea to carry around the bare and hollow skull of the monk **Sergius**—a companion of **Muhammad**—as a relic, in order to obtain offerings and alms from pious and simple-minded people. As the inventor of the fraud described to his companions the monk to whom the skull supposedly belonged, he painted him with all the features that fit **Holzinger** <note>Holzinger was the monk and court favorite in Württemberg who had previously persecuted Reuchlin.</note> *).

During the time that passed from his return to his fatherland until his acceptance of the dignity of a league judge <note>German: *Bankrichterwürde*. Reuchlin served as a judge for the Swabian League, a powerful defensive alliance in the Holy Roman Empire, from 1502 to 1513.</note>, Reuchlin was most active as a writer. Even if he had not found relaxation himself in scholarly investigations and compositions, the urgency of his friends would have compelled him to do so. They pleaded with him—verbally, in writing, or through special messengers—that he might remedy their intolerable ignorance and publish now something in Greek, now something in Hebrew for them *). The desire to serve his friends, but even more so to serve religion, drove him to prepare his *Rudimenta linguæ Hebraicæ* <note>original: "Rudiments of the Hebrew Language"</note>, or his Hebrew grammar and dictionary. These appeared in the spring of 1506 in Pforzheim and were received with the greatest acclaim throughout Europe, standing out among Reuchlin’s many works **). Even before Reuchlin had this work printed—which belongs among the most remarkable scholarly occurrences of the 16th century—he wrote several other small essays that must not be overlooked. In the year 1502, a plague so terrible raged in Upper Germany that Reuchlin did not know where to save himself. In this distress, the Provost of Denkendorf

...lead [them] and thereby prepare them for the recognition of their errors. Such a great and lasting divine punishment, which has afflicted the Jews for over 1400 years, could only have been incurred by sins that this people never committed before; and these sins were none other than that they killed the true Messiah and continue to blaspheme him.

"In many ways," says Reuchlin on the sixth page, "they have blasphemed, reviled, and disgraced Him, for the reason that they brought Him to death because He allowed himself to be called a King—that is, the Messiah—and a Son of God. Thereby they have attempted to thrust the lie down the throat of Almighty God and make God a liar, who spoke through the prophet Isaiah in the 66th Chapter: *If I cause to be born, should I not also bring forth? says the Lord. If I cause to bring forth, should I be barren? says your God.* <note>Isaiah 66:9</note>. By this they were well warned that God considers it a disgrace that He should not have a son, as if He were powerless and barren, and should not be like other fathers. For a human begets a human, and a cow a calf. But no human by nature may beget a donkey, nor a lion a lamb. But God has begotten. That is His Messiah, as He says in the second Psalm, beginning thus: *Why do the heathens rage and the people speak words of scorn? The rulers of the lands stand up and the leaders consult with one another against God and His Messiah.* <note>Psalm 2:1-2</note>. And immediately after, that same Messiah says: *God has spoken to me: You are my son, today I have begotten you.* <note>Psalm 2:7</note>. That is, from eternity. Since they have now blasphemed Almighty God as if He were a liar, powerless, and barren, so follows one blasphemy from the—

Reuchlin's opponents later accused him, not without reason, that in his letter he had indicted the Jews as persistent blasphemers and as constant enemies of Christians and the Christian religion.

"They call him (the Messiah) a sinner and a sorcerer, and 'the disgraced one' <note>original: "geschendten", often a derogatory reference to the crucifixion</note>. And the kind Virgin Mary they call *Haria* <note>a derogatory Hebrew play on the name Maria, meaning 'excrement' or 'fury'</note>, and the disciples or apostles they call heretics. And us Christians they call a 'non-people' or 'no people,' and foolish heathens, and many other evil words which they cast out. From this it is to be noted that this sin of blasphemy is the greatest and highest against God; therefore the characteristic of the first part mentioned above—regarding the sin for which they have been punished so long—would be clearly found. The second part—that all Jews at this time, as long as they remain Jews, are complicit in such blasphemy and take a special joy in it when they can devise and invent something for shame and vice—is manifest in all their deeds and omissions and in their customary prayer. Also in their books which they wrote and read against us, all from the book *Nizahon* <note>Sefer Nizzahon, a medieval Jewish apologetic work often used in Christian-Jewish polemics</note> and *Brüdersol* <note>likely a reference to the polemical text "Puder Scholl" or "Pudur Scholl"</note>, also in the prayer *uleschumadim* <note>original Hebrew: "v'lamalshinim" or "v'lamshumadim", referring to the "Birkat ha-Minim," a prayer against heretics and apostates</note>, which is well to be noted."

<meta>This page concludes the biographical narrative of Johann Reuchlin, detailing his final return to his homeland, his last teaching position at the University of Tübingen, his death in 1522, and a summary of his personal character and legacy.</meta>

...soon from Ingolstadt; and now he returned to his homeland, which at least was no longer a theater of war. As soon as the rumor of his return spread, the University of Tübingen sent deputies to meet him, who were tasked with inviting him to teach at the homeland’s <term>high school (university)</term> just as he had previously taught in Ingolstadt. Reuchlin gave in to these requests. He first instructed the youth in Hebrew and Greek grammar, and then intended to explain the Hebrew Bible, along with the speech of Demosthenes *On the Crown*, and the counter-speech of Aeschines \*), when in the summer of the year 1522, he was overcome by a lingering illness, which took him away on July 30th in the 67th year of his age in Stuttgart, where he had been brought. He bequeathed his library to the College at Pforzheim, where it was to be set up in the church and opened for everyone’s use. Most of the books left behind by Reuchlin were subsequently carried off by the Capuchin friars to Weil der Stadt or Cologne and consumed by the flames of war. Some of the most precious manuscripts are still present in Karlsruhe today.

Johann Reuchlin did at least as much honor to the sciences through his character and his life as he had to thank them for the formation of his character. He was a tender husband, brother, and relative; a steadfast and helpful friend; an incorruptible and indefatigable advocate, judge, and businessman; a diligent and faithful teacher of

<meta>This page continues the character portrait of Johann Reuchlin, focusing on his motivations for reviving Hebrew studies and his defense against accusations of being bribed by the Jewish community.</meta>

<page-num>80</page-num>
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

...worthy adversary. Reuchlin's dominant inclination and unceasing effort was the improvement of the sciences of his time, especially the restoration of the study of ancient languages and philosophy, and most of all the renewal of Hebrew literature and the improvement of the degenerated <term>theology (divine learning)</term> arising from the study of the original sources. In these efforts for the reception and dissemination of better knowledge, Reuchlin was not fired by vain ambition, nor by self-interest, but—like all great heroes of truth and virtue in that age—by genuine love for humanity and piety; and he therefore sacrificed time, money, labor, and even a part of his reputation for the cause of truth and religion. 

"I have pursued nothing," he writes to Cardinal Hadrian <margin>\*) In the dedication of the book *On the Accents and Orthography of the Hebrew Language*, pages 2, 3.</margin>, "with such great exertion and such a desire as the study of ancient languages; for which reason I do not doubt that I have obeyed the hints of the <term>genius (inner spirit)</term> driving me. No part of my life has passed, nor passes even now, in which I do not occupy myself with something aimed at the expansion of ancient wisdom and the languages in which it is contained." 

After Reuchlin briefly mentioned his works in Basel and in the times following, he continues: "I used this opportunity to learn Hebrew, which I still lacked. At no small cost, I purchased the instruction of every learned Jewish scholar from whom I could hope to learn something. I applied myself to the Hebrew language not only because it gives me pleasure, but because I foresaw the great benefit it would have for

<column-break/>

<page-num>81</page-num>
<sig>Volume I. F</sig>

for religion and true theology. To these, I had already previously directed all my scholarly works, and from then on, I directed them even more. As a faithful worshiper of our Savior, I did everything for the restoration and glorification of the true Christian Church. No thirst for gold drove me to the study of Hebrew literature; rather, I had to expend much gold to become acquainted with it. Nor was it a desire for fame; for on the contrary, I had to hide these studies because many believed they were not fitting for the dignity <note>Reuchlin held high legal and political offices, and studying Hebrew was often viewed with suspicion by the conservative clergy.</note> which I held. 

Certainly, my sublime patron, it is not self-interest which draws me there, but my inclination and piety. I swear by the precious blood of Christ, who gave himself as a sacrifice for us, that I have never received from the Jews either gold or silver, nor other gifts, and that even in the long-lasting war which I lead against so many and so rich <term>beggars (mendicant monks)</term> <note>This refers to the mendicant orders, such as the Dominicans, who were Reuchlin's primary opponents in the controversy over Jewish books.</note>, I have received support from no man. And yet there are people who dare to assert that I am bribed by the Jews with I know not how much gold. However, I await the Lord with confidence, who will put all lying mouths to shame. Under the guidance of the Lord, I continue to learn the ancient languages more and more even as an old man, because I am convinced that no other works of the human spirit contribute so much to the explanation of the Holy Scriptures and laws as the knowledge and gift of languages." \*) When has ever, writes

Reuchlin to the Emperor Maximilian \*), would a court jester <note>original: "Schalksnarr"</note> at court ever accuse a dishonorable man of such things as the Cologne professors charge me with, an innocent man? I, who in my entire life have never offended a single one of them, neither in word nor in deed? I, who according to the judgment of all those who know me, am not only free from all bad actions, but also from the smallest suspicion of them, and—if it could be done without envy or proud arrogance—would boldly compete with the most virtuous men of our time for the fame of the greatest integrity †)? How pure and noble must the man have known himself to be, who could speak in such a way to an enlightened Emperor in the sight of all Germany!

His contemporaries, who praised Reuchlin as the **Phoenix of his century**, as the **glory of his fatherland**, and as the **teacher of his people** \*), admired in him a rare gift and fortune: that he was just as great a businessman and statesman as he was a scholar and writer \*\*).

Reuchlin was a judge for the <term>Swabian League (a powerful mutual defense alliance of cities and nobles in Southern Germany)</term> for eleven years; for over thirty years he was a counselor, ambassador, or legal consultant to two emperors and many other German princes and cities †), as well as the advocate for countless distinguished families and private individuals. In all these roles, Reuchlin accomplished so much good through his spirit, his learning and integrity, his diligence, and his great connections within and outside of Germany—and prevented so much evil—that one might become uncertain whether he benefited his fellow man more through his active life or through his teaching and writing ††). <meta>This page transitions from a discussion of Reuchlin’s public service as a statesman to a detailed evaluation of his impact as a scholar. It sets the scene of the "sad state" of German education in the 15th century, characterized by stagnant Scholasticism, before Reuchlin and his contemporaries began the work of the Northern Renaissance.</meta>

<page-num>84</page-num>

Posterity values the merits that Reuchlin earned in his public life only imperfectly and in general terms. But He, who has **counted every hair on our heads**, counted also all these good works of Reuchlin; their consequences are lost neither for Reuchlin nor for the world, even if we cannot oversee them as easily as we do Reuchlin’s own writings.

Regarding Reuchlin as a scholar, both his education and his merits as a teacher and writer are worthy of being examined particularly.

In Reuchlin's youth—and one might say throughout the entire fifteenth century—the secondary schools and universities, and the sciences taught at both, were in the same dismal state into which they had sunk since the beginning of the thirteenth century. All the changes in scholarship and public instruction that had occurred in Italy over several generations had not had the slightest influence on German schools and academic sciences. A good Latin writing style and the great Roman authors were just as unknown in German schools as the Hebrew and Greek languages and literature. Even at the start of the sixteenth century, philosophy consisted of a web of <term>sophisms (clever but misleading arguments)</term> to which a person's entire life was not long enough to master \*). Theology,

His legal expertise aided many cities and princes, and everyone found him to be honest and faithful.<- <note>original Latin: "theologi faciunt Reuchlin sicut scribæ et Pharisæi fecerunt Christo..."</note>

</margin>

jurisprudence, and medicine, even in Italy and France, were still such a chaos of subtle disputes and problems as they had been for three centuries. among scholars, whoever wished to advance had to visit the universities in France and Italy; and if Reuchlin had not been granted the opportunity, he would have learned neither the pure Roman language <note>Referring to classical Latin as opposed to medieval Scholastic Latin.</note> nor Greek literature, at least not as early as he later taught them in Germany and France. Italian universities maintained a decisive advantage over all others, especially German schools, throughout the entire fifteenth century and even in the first fifth of the sixteenth; for this reason, all noble and spirited youths were sent by their princes, parents, or relatives to the universities of Italy as the only or best dwellings for useful knowledge *).

*) "You write," writes Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), an influential Italian humanist and philosopher.</note> to Reuchlin in *Reuchlin’s Letters*, Book I, page 7, "that the princes of Germany, in your name, are sending youths to Florence to be educated as if to an Academy." <note>original Latin: "Scribitis... ad nos vestroque nomine Germaniae principes Florentiam adolescentes erudiendos tanquam ad Academiam mittere."</note> Ulrich von Hutten says in his poem *On Un-degenerate Germany*: "Therefore, everyone travels to the regions of Italy to bring back the cultivation of the mind, the commerce of the Latin tongue, and the arts of the Greeks." <note>original Latin: "Ergo adit Italiae quisque loca, ut adferat inde ingenii cultum, et latiae commercia linguae Graecorumque artes."</note> *Hutten’s Poems*, p. 108. "For when I—whether from a desire to argue or rather out of a love for the truth—placed the training grounds <note>The author uses "palæstras," a Greek term for a wrestling school, here meaning a place of intellectual exercise.</note> of Italy, which I might call the nurses, authors, and creators of the best arts, not only before the German ones but before the whole world, my brother, being a man of singular love for his fatherland, took this poorly; he tried to compare your Tübingen with the Italian Academies, provided that the study of humane letters <note>A term for the humanities or classical studies.</note> did not flee so much from there." <note>original Latin: "Namque cum ego seu studio contradicendi... modo humanarum litterarum studia istic non adeo fugerent."</note> He encourages Reuchlin to persuade Count Eberhard to introduce ancient literature in Tübingen. What Reuchlin could not achieve in his homeland, he accomplished in Saxony; for the Elector Frederick founded the University of Wittenberg with Reuchlin’s advice (page 271 of Melanchthon's Declaration, cited above), which in a few years became the headquarters not only of a purer theology, but also of a better philosophy and ancient literature. As soon as Wittenberg flourished, the travel of noble and wealthy students to Italy and France became much rarer.

<column-break/>

<page-num>87</page-num>

The necessity of seeking better knowledge at great risk and expense at foreign universities was not the only difficulty opposing the education of noble youth in Reuchlin’s era. An equally great obstacle lay in the cost and rarity of books, which persisted until the end of the fifteenth century, despite the fact that the art of printing had already been invented for over a generation and spread throughout Europe. "I am sending you," writes Hieronymus of Sparta to Reuchlin in the year 1478, "the Greek grammar of Theodore <note>Theodore Gaza, a key figure in the revival of Greek learning.</note>. The lexicon you ask for does not belong to me but to a good friend, and is said to cost six gold crowns. The fables you once saw at my place are not for sale. I do, however, possess a copy I made myself, and this is at your service if you desire it." *) "You are angry with me," Petrus Jacobi of Arlon replied to Reuchlin in 1488 from Pavia, "that I have sent you no Greek books. But you ask the impossible of me. I have crawled through every bookstore and found plenty of Greek children <note>likely a humorous or metaphorical reference to Greeks themselves or perhaps basic primers.</note>, but no Greek books. I even asked my teachers, and they are astonished at the supply of Greek works you possess. Even Georg Merula, one of Italy’s greatest scholars, admires your wealth of Greek books and says he would hate to be without many of those scholars. If you desire a Greek dictionary or the grammar of Chrysoloras <note>Manuel Chrysoloras, whose grammar was the first used in Western Europe.</note>, let me know. I am sending you now the best I found among three hundred books, bought at a high price..."

The book trade was still so poorly established many years afterward that a learned prior of the Ottobeuren monastery <note>A Benedictine monastery in Bavaria known for its library.</note> complained to Reuchlin in the year 1512: he had given orders to all booksellers far and wide to buy him a Greek Bible, which, however, he had not yet been able to obtain \*). When Philipp Melanchthon <note>A famous reformer and educator, and Reuchlin’s great-nephew.</note> lectured on the speeches of Demosthenes <note>An ancient Greek statesman and orator.</note> in Wittenberg in the year 1524, he had only four listeners, because absolutely no copies of the Greek orator were to be found. The four listeners, who were not deterred by this, had to make copies for themselves from their teacher's single volume \*\*).

Even if Reuchlin had not led such a beneficial public life, nor acquired such great fame through his writings as he actually did, he would still deserve as much praise and gratitude from the Germans as a teacher of youth as Johann von Ravenna <note>Giovanni Malpaghini (c. 1346–1417), an influential early Italian humanist teacher who taught many famous scholars.</note> received in Italy. Reuchlin was the first among the Germans who taught not only pure Latin, and besides this the Greek and Hebrew languages, but also a purer Aristotelian philosophy in Basel, Orleans, Poitiers, Ingolstadt, and Tübingen. Among these universities, Basel was probably the one where Reuchlin provided the greatest benefit, because he stayed here the longest and occupied himself almost entirely with the in-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Johannes Reuchlin’s immense influence.
