As great as the fame and merits of Reuchlin were as a man of affairs <note>The original German "Geschäftsmannes" here refers to his high-ranking roles as a judge, diplomat, and legal advisor for the Swabian League.</note> and as a public teacher, both were—in the judgment of his contemporaries—infinitely surpassed by his literary fame and merits. Everything Reuchlin wrote was admired as a supreme masterpiece: his German works as much as his Latin ones; his poetry as much as his prose; his translations as much as his original compositions; and his polemical writings as much as his instructional ones. This admiration for Reuchlin as a writer reached the level of adoration, not only in Germany but also in Italy, France, and England; letters written by Reuchlin were kissed and preserved like sacred relics\*). After his death, Erasmus placed him among the saints in the *Apotheosis of Capnion* <note>The title "Apotheosis Capnionis" refers to Reuchlin’s Greek nickname, "Capnion," which means "Little Smoke," a play on his German name "Rauch" (Smoke).</note> and wrote his name alongside that of St. Jerome, both because of his gift for the three ancient languages <note>Latin, Greek, and Hebrew.</note> and because of the persecutions he endured, which he shared in common with Jerome\*). Despite this universal admiration from his contemporaries, a sincere admirer and estimator of Reuchlin's merits cannot hide the fact that Reuchlin wrote German much less skillfully than Ulrich von Hutten or Luther. Furthermore, his Latin style was neither as pure nor as correct as that of Erasmus, Agricola, Hutten, and Melanchthon; and his Latin poems were very much inferior to those of other poets of that time, particularly those of Eobanus Hessus.

...far lagged behind; and that among all of Reuchlin's works, there is not a single one that would still be read today, or deserve to be read, either for the sake of its beautiful language or because of the many new and important truths it contains. The most useful among his writings are the *Rudiments of the Hebrew Language* <note>original: *rudimenta Linguae Hebraicae*</note>, not only because he thereby made it possible for the inquisitive to learn the Hebrew language without further oral instruction and led them to the study of the holy books in their original tongue, but also because through frequent improvements to the Vulgate <note>The Vulgate was the standard Latin translation of the Bible used by the Catholic Church for centuries.</note> and to several <term>Schriftgelehrten|scholars of scripture</term> who were considered infallible, he drew attention to the errors of both and thus prepared the way for the restoration of true theology <note>original: *Gottesgelahrtheit*</note> \*). Reuchlin foresaw the reproaches that would be made against him for his boldness in criticizing the Vulgate and the interpretations of famous doctors <note>The "Doctors of the Church" were authoritative theological teachers whose writings were often treated as law.</note>. He sought to counter these reproaches, but he could not prevent himself from being subsequently accused of heresy or grave errors because of them \*\*).

However highly one may value the benefit that Reuchlin established through the awakening and rapid spread of the study of the Hebrew language, it certainly does not outweigh the damage caused by Reuchlin's writings *On the Miraculous Word* <note>original: *de verbo mirifico*</note> and *On the Cabbalistic Art* <note>original: *de arte cabbalistica*</note>. In following generations, whenever magic and the Cabbala were attacked, it was always primarily Count Johann Picus of Mirandula <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Italian Renaissance philosopher who sought to reconcile Christianity with other philosophies.</note> and Reuchlin whose well-known piety and scholarship were used to justify and protect the disputed superstitions.

Fortunately for the world and for his own fame, the conflict which the Cologne theologians <term>Gottesgelehrten|scholars of divinity or theologians</term> began with Reuchlin over the fate of Jewish books more than made up for all the harm Reuchlin had done through his Cabbalistic writings. The history of this conflict is more important for the history of science and religion at the beginning of the sixteenth century than everything else I have related so far regarding Reuchlin's merits.

Reuchlin’s dispute with the Cologne theologians was by no means caused by motives as significant and deep-seated as those for which it was later continued. Reuchlin and his friends took it as a well-known fact \*) that the Cologne theologians attacked and persecuted Reuchlin not so much as a defender of Jewish writings, but rather as one of the foremost awakeners of ancient literature in general, and especially of the study of the Hebrew language; and that they wished to destroy not only other Jewish books but also the Holy Scriptures, in order to suppress the truth itself along with the sources of truth—

...suppress, and to be able to continue asserting their rule, founded on deception and error, undisturbed. In all the documents of the dispute, I find no trace of such intentions by the Cologne group at the beginning of their war with Reuchlin. Rather, the Dominican Order used Reuchlin as their advocate, wrote him the most polite letters of thanks, and showed him favors wherever possible \*). Even from the letters that Reuchlin wrote to the theologians in Cologne after the publication of his *Eyeglass* <note>original: *Augenspiegel*, Reuchlin's 1511 defense against accusations of heresy</note>, and from the responses of the latter \*\*), it is clear that the Cologne group had harbored no particular grudge against Reuchlin until then, and that he had not feared any such thing.

Small and common passions of uneducated or corrupt people, and accidental circumstances, ignited the first spark and fanned it into a mighty flame. As this flame spread further and further, breaking out into a general, consuming fire, it naturally seized upon much that initially seemed exposed to no danger at all. In the course of the battle, the first occasion for it was forgotten; and both contending parties sought—as also happened in the Reformation that followed soon after—to achieve entirely different goals than those by which they had first been driven against each other.

The first occasion for the dispute, which I will now describe, was a baptized Jew, **Johann Pfefferkorn**, without whom Reuchlin would never have been involved in a war with the Cologne theologians. This **Johann Pfefferkorn** converted to the Christian religion in Cologne in the year 1506 \*), and from that moment on—partly through the zeal he showed for his new faith and against his former coreligionists, and partly, as rumor had it, through the charms of his wife—he became a beloved client of his converters, the Dominicans in Cologne, who subsequently secured him several lucrative positions \*\*). The new convert was not without knowledge, although Reuchlin showed Pfefferkorn Hebrew books which the latter could not read. Nor was he entirely without a head for things, at least when it came to insults and slander †). For the rest, after his baptism, he remained entirely "Jewish" in the negative sense of the word ††) <note>The author here reflects the common prejudices of his time, equating certain negative traits with Jewishness despite the conversion.</note>; that is, full of schemes to satisfy his greed, revenge, or other low passions. In any case, Johann Pfefferkorn published several writings concerning the conversion of the Jews in the first years after his change of religion. This is rightly concluded not only from the diverging and even contradictory principles they contain but also from the fact that some are written in German and others in Latin—a language that their alleged author, Johann Pfefferkorn, did not understand \*\*). **little book** has three sections. In the first, the author endeavors to show the Jews their previous errors, as well as the groundlessness of their continued expectation of the Messiah, and to remove their doubts regarding the truth of the Christian religion or the transition to Christianity. In the second, he explains the obstacles that have hitherto opposed the conversion of the Jews; he finds the primary obstacles in the practice of <term>usury|the practice of lending money at interest, often the only profession legally permitted to Jews at the time</term>, for the abolition of which he therefore encourages the Christian authorities; and then in the <term>Talmudic|referring to the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism</term> and other books, which reinforce the Jews in their errors. For this reason, he likewise exhorts the Christian governments to take these dangerous books away from the Jews and leave them only the Bible \*). In this same section, the author defends the Jews against many hateful accusations made against them at the time by the Christian common folk—against the stealing and slaughtering of Christian children, and so on <note>This refers to the "blood libel," a false and violent antisemitic myth that Jews murdered Christian children for ritual purposes.</note>. In the third section, the author also invites conversion to the Christian religion by claiming the end of the world is imminent, when there will be only one shepherd, one flock, and one faith. As signs of the coming Day of Judgment, or at least a great change in things, he views the frequent conversions of the Jews and, among other things, the total corruption of morals and institutions. "It is," he says, "as we clearly see, that there is little or no obedience or respect for superiors left. The lowest wish to be placed on a level with, or even above, the highest."

In conclusion, Reuchlin cites the detrimental consequences that would inevitably arise from a violent seizure and burning of Jewish books. If we were to rob the Jews of their writings by force, they would certainly say that we were afraid of them, and that we took away their defenses and weapons because we could not withstand them. Reuchlin's sealed legal opinion, which was intended only for the **Elector of Mainz** and for the Emperor, soon fell into the hands of **Johann Pfefferkorn** and the **Dominicans** in **Cologne**. <note>The Dominicans of Cologne were the leaders of the conservative theological opposition to Reuchlin.</note> In his *Augenspiegel*, where Reuchlin still wanted to spare the Cologne theologians, he merely says that he did not know how Johann Pfefferkorn and his wife had obtained his sealed opinion *). to read the opinion. Although he was entitled to this right, he was not entitled to another which he presumed for himself: the right to make public use of Reuchlin's opinion to disparage its author. Pfefferkorn wrote, with the help of the Cologne theologians <note>Refers to the Dominican order in Cologne, who were the primary opponents of Hebrew studies at the time.</note>, a defamatory pamphlet against Reuchlin under the title *Handspiegel* [Hand Mirror], and sold this libelous work at the Frankfurt Spring Fair in the year 1511. In his *Handspiegel*, Pfefferkorn sought not only to refute Reuchlin's legal opinion, but he also accused him of a criminal favoring of the Jews and Jewish blasphemy, as well as many dubious or dangerous errors. Reuchlin complained about this "scandalous little book," as he called it, to Emperor Maximilian, whom he attended to for this matter in the city of Reutlingen \*). The Emperor expressed his horror at the outrage of his solicitor <note>Pfefferkorn held a minor imperial appointment to oversee the book confiscations.</note> through both words and gestures \*\*). But because Maximilian was in a great hurry at that time, he could not investigate Reuchlin's complaint or have it investigated; and the Emperor's advisors promised Reuchlin that their master would commission the Bishop of Augsburg to investigate this matter. Reuchlin waited for a time in vain for a summons from the Bishop, who had been announced to him as the imperial commissioner. Since the summons still failed to appear, he had inquiries made with the Bishop to see if the latter would accept the complaint against Johannes Pfefferkorn; to which he received the answer, however, that nothing from the imperial court concerning Reuchlin and Pfefferkorn had been assigned to him.

Following this notice, Reuchlin saw himself forced to take up the defense of his attacked honor himself: especially since he had to fear that Pfefferkorn and his wife would continue to sell the remaining copies of the *Handspiegel* at the upcoming Michaelmas Fair <note>A major autumn trade fair held around late September.</note>. Therefore, to save his good name, he had a protective writing printed against Pfefferkorn under the title *Augenspiegel* [Eye Mirror], which was bought with great eagerness at the Autumn Fair in 1511 and read throughout all of Germany. Besides a short narrative of the reasons for his legal opinion and the opinion itself, this *Augenspiegel* also contained a Latin explanation of the latter in scholastic form, and a refutation of Pfefferkorn's *Handspiegel*, the contents of which he reduced to thirty-four untruths. The largest and most hateful of the untruths of which Reuchlin accused Pfefferkorn were the following: That Reuchlin denied the blasphemies of the Jews and excused Jewish usury; that he had taken money from them and, for the sake of base profit, had attacked not only Pfefferkorn but also the most famous teachers of the Franciscan and Dominican orders; that he understood no Hebrew and yet boasted of his knowledge of this language, although it could be proven that Reuchlin had not written his Hebrew grammar himself; that there were many wicked parts in him, etc.

In the letter to Conrad Rollin, or Conrad of Ulm, Reuchlin briefly recounts what has happened so far and shares a concise summary of his legal opinion <note>original: "Gutachtens"; referring to the official recommendation Reuchlin wrote for the Emperor regarding whether Jewish books should be seized.</note>. Regarding Pfefferkorn <note>Johannes Pfefferkorn, a Jewish convert to Christianity and vocal advocate for the destruction of the Talmud.</note>, he says that he did not want so much to burn the books of the Jews as to confiscate them, in order to share in the gold with which the Jews would certainly have redeemed their books. According to common rumor, this same Pfefferkorn had been incited against Reuchlin by the Dominican Order, and particularly by the Prior of the Dominicans in Cologne, Jacob Hogstraten <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a notorious inquisitor and Reuchlin’s primary antagonist.</note>. He is being accused from all sides of now receiving this "thanks" for the long and manifold services he has rendered to the Order. He, Reuchlin, could not yet possibly give credence to these common rumors, as he was aware that he had always served the Order faithfully and had hitherto been deemed worthy of special favor and a close connection with the Order.

Arnold von Tungern and Conrad Rollin handed over the letters received from Reuchlin to the theological faculty in Cologne, and the faculty replied to Reuchlin on January 2, 1512, in a separate letter. In this letter, an apparent zeal for the Christian religion, an apparent paternal seriousness toward an erring son of the Church, and an apparent mildness and leniency toward unintentional missteps were masterfully combined *). No passage in the Faculty’s letter was more striking to Reuchlin, and none was less in keeping with the monkish cunning of the Cologne theologians, than the passage in which the Faculty stated that Reuchlin had sought to disrupt the successfully initiated business against the books of the Jews through his legal opinion <note>original: "Gutachten"; Reuchlin's formal recommendation to Emperor Maximilian I regarding whether Jewish books should be seized.</note>. In his response to the Faculty in Cologne, Reuchlin let nothing show of the impression this statement had made on him. Rather, he gave thanks for the paternal mildness with which they intended to bear and correct his missteps. He repeated his devotion to the Catholic Church, his childlike reverence for the Fathers in Cologne, and his ignorance of "theological subtleties"—an expression Rollin had used in his last letter—and finally begged most urgently that they would share with him the new explanations, or the expansions of old ones, which they required of him *). In his reply to Rollin, he justified himself with greater confidence regarding the accusations the Faculty had made against him. He claimed it was impossible for him to have intended to disrupt the business started against the Jewish books, as he had known nothing of it when composing his legal opinion. The Faculty in Cologne grew weary of the letters and counter-letters, and declared to Reuchlin once and for all that they were not yet satisfied by anything he had said or done. These latest demands and threats from the Cologne group finally caused Reuchlin to find his courage. In his replies to the theological faculty and to Rollin, there is no longer any visible anxiety, nor any assumed humility or reverence. He writes as a man who is conscious of his innocence as well as his strength; who is ready to do everything to maintain peace, but who also refuses to be forced into any step unworthy of him. Because Reuchlin wrote in these letters as he thought and as he ought to think, they are much more truthful, or more natural and calm, than any he had sent until then.

Since he had not succeeded, he wrote to the theological faculty <margin>**) p. 134. 135.</margin>, through all his pleas in getting the Faculty to provide him with a formula by which he could have resolved the alleged offense, he intended to try whether he might prevent all caused misunderstandings and satisfy the theological faculty in a new German explanation, which was to appear in the upcoming spring fair <note>The Frankfurt Book Fair, the most important event for the German book trade.</note>. From that moment on, he gave up all thoughts of peace and rejoiced in the consciousness that his cause was just and that his weapons were not blunt <margin>*) In the place cited.</margin>. To refute the Cologne slanderers, he wrote his **Defense against the Cologne Slanderers** <note>original: "defensio contra Calumniatores Colonienses"</note>, which he dedicated to Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor, who initially supported Reuchlin's scholarly mission but was pressured by the Church.</note> and published during the Easter or Lenten fair in Frankfurt in the year 1513 <margin>**) Van der Hardt, History of the Reformation, Part II, pp. 53–93.</margin>. In this defense, he once again demolished the defamatory accusations of the Cologne group: That he had recommended the godless Jewish people, their faith, their rabbis, and their books to the detriment of the Christian religion; that he sought to save the Talmud <term>Talmud: a central text of Rabbinic Judaism containing legal and theological discussions</term> and other godless and shameful fictions of the Jews; that he sought to win over the Jews through flattery, to hide their true nature, and to excuse their usury; that he had spoken disrespectfully of Catholic teachers; that as an inconstant and fearful man, he had wounded the hearts of the faithful through his excuses and skirmishing; that out of anxious confusion he had slandered the Church of God; that he had falsely cited Saint Paul as a witness; that he had even brought in legal scholars against Christ and the Catholic Church; that he had given free rein to his wit to the dishonor of Christ; and that his assertions in general tasted of heresy. However, Reuchlin did not merely accuse the Cologne theologians of twisting his words—which had been so often and so precisely defined—against all rules of the Christian religion and all duties of Christian teachers, and of maliciously turning his defensive

Reuchlin relied neither on the justice of his cause nor on the thoroughness of his defense alone. <meta>Continuity: This page continues the history of the "Reuchlin Affair," detailing how the legal and theological dispute between Johannes Reuchlin and the Cologne Dominicans transformed into a broad intellectual and cultural movement across Europe, setting the stage for the Reformation.</meta>

<page-num>144</page-num>

Through the efforts of Reuchlin and his friends, starting in the year 1513, an alliance arose—first in Germany, and soon also in Italy, France, and England. In this league, all friends of ancient literature, all enlightened legal scholars, physicians, and secular clergy <note>Priests who lived in the world (the "saeculum") rather than in monasteries.</note> united to defend Reuchlin against the attacks of the Cologne party. This alliance expanded and strengthened all the more as Reuchlin’s dangers and the violence of his enemies increased. Soon, the entire youth, thirsty for better knowledge, the best and most enlightened princes and knights, and the largest and most powerful Imperial Cities were drawn into this league. They fought against the mendicant monks through collective appeals to the courts, through collaborative literary works, and finally through open force. Indeed, from the point in time mentioned, the struggle was no longer about the fate of the Jews and Jewish books, but about the victory of the new light over the old darkness. During this conflict, and because of it, all of civilized Europe divided into two

---

> <note>original: "qui non modo saeculares litteras et doctores exosos habent..."</note> "They not only hold secular letters and teachers in hatred, but these swiftest of beasts also rail against secular priests, so that they may drag them into the hatred of the common people with the greatest ignominy, the more easily to fill their own purses." Letters of Reuchlin, Book II, p. 216. Given the unwavering grace that Maximilian always showed to Reuchlin, it is not at all probable that this Emperor repeatedly banned Reuchlin’s writings against the Cologne party, as Majus (p. 345 in *The Life of Reuchlin*) recounts based on a false claim by Reuchlin’s accusers (see *Acts of the Jews*, edited by von der Hardt, p. 121). In the following pages, several examples will occur showing that Hogstraten <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, the chief Inquisitor of Cologne and Reuchlin's primary antagonist.</note> allowed himself the grossest falsehoods even in public and legal documents. After the publication of the <term>Eye-Mirror</term> <note>Original: *Augenspiegel*; Reuchlin’s 1511 book defending the preservation of Jewish texts.</note>, Maximilian issued *letters of inhibition* <note>original: "litteras inhibitorias"; a legal stay or restraining order.</note>, whereby both parties, especially Hogstraten, were commanded to abstain from public polemics and were directed toward the path of legal recourse. See the letters of Peutinger in Reuchlin’s *Letters*, Vol. II, p. 187.

parties: the party of the Reuchlinists, or the friends of truth; and the party of the Cologne theologians, or the enemies of genuine scholarship. During this struggle, and because of it, the greatest changes occurred in the organization of the universities, in the sciences taught there, and in the studies of the youth. Through these changes, the mindset of the European nations was altered, and the Reformation was prepared and, one might say in a certain sense, brought about. Because of the many consequences important for religion and science that were foreseen as the necessary result of the conflict, Reuchlin’s friends soon began to consider it a special act of Providence that this struggle had been raised at that very time, and specifically against Reuchlin, because anyone else would have necessarily succumbed *). "I thank the grace of God," Luther wrote to Reuchlin **), "which has been revealed in you, dear man, and which has strengthened you so that you have been able to stop the mouths of the unrighteous. You were a tool of God without knowing it, yet most welcome to all friends of a purer theology. God directed everything differently than it was begun by you. <meta>Continuity: This page continues the history of the "Reuchlin Affair," specifically highlighting how the personal defense of Johannes Reuchlin against the Cologne Dominicans evolved into a unified front of European humanists fighting for academic and religious freedom.</meta>

I am always present with you through my wishes and my prayer. What I could not do then as your fellow combatant, now happens to me in full measure as your successor. The teeth of that Behemoth <note>Behemoth: A powerful biblical beast, here used to represent the aggressive and monstrous nature of Reuchlin's institutional enemies.</note> now also fall upon me, to wipe away the disgrace they incurred through their struggle with you. They do not fight with reasons, but with open violence. Yet Christ still lives, and I can lose nothing, since I possess nothing. The horns of these bulls <note>A biblical metaphor for powerful, aggressive enemies, likely referencing Psalm 22:12.</note> have been broken not a little by your strength. God has worked through you so that the tyrannical sophists <note>Sophists: A derogatory term used by humanists for Scholastic theologians who focused on complex logic and dogma rather than the direct study of ancient texts or scripture.</note> finally learned to oppose the study of authentic theology with a bit more caution, so that Germany—suppressed and nearly annihilated for so many centuries by school-theology <term>Scholasticism: The dominant medieval method of learning that emphasized philosophical logic and tradition over the historical and linguistic study of the Bible.</term>—could begin to breathe more freely again. The beginning of better knowledge could only be made by a man of exceptional divine gifts. Just as God (if I may venture this comparison) crushed the greatest of all mountains, Christ, into the dust of death, and yet from this dust so many great mountains grew; so too would you have brought forth less fruit if you had not been humbled to the dust. For this very reason, so many defenders of the holy doctrines and scriptures are now rising up everywhere. And the prayer of the sighing Church has been heard: *Save me, Lord,* etc. <note>original: "Errette mich, Herr, u. s. w." Reference to Psalm 12:1.</note> — Each of the primary events just mentioned deserves to be set in a brighter light.

defenders, Reuchlin. The following testimonies will leave no doubt about the existence of such a league in the years 1514, 1515, 1518, and so on.

You will surely be victorious, writes the poet Eobanus Hessus in January 1515 to Reuchlin *), and just as surely we will triumph with you. The senate of the learned republic <note>The "Republic of Letters": a conceptual community of scholars across Europe who shared common intellectual values regardless of nationality.</note> has already decreed your triumph. Hutten, Buschius, Crotus, Spalatinus, Melanchthon, and many others will sing of your victory with me, and I will awaken several here in Erfurt who will so harass those terrifying figures or monsters that they shall have no more rest on land or sea. — All of us, reports Petrejus Aprobacchus from Rome in the same year, who have dedicated ourselves to the service of Minerva <note>Minerva: The Roman goddess of wisdom and the arts, used here to represent the humanist commitment to classical learning.</note>, must watch and fight for you as our general. For Reuchlin’s cause and for the expansion and strengthening of the Reuchlinian League, none were more active than Willibald Pirkheimer, Ulrich von Hutten, and Count Hermann von Neuenar (also known as *de nova Aquila*), the Cathedral Provost in Cologne. "Buschius and Hutten," writes the Count of Neuenar **), "are the most zealous defenders of your honor. Glarean wrote to me recently that in his regions, many are fighting for you. But I do not even believe that one needs so many auxiliary troops against a few frogs <note>Frogs: A common humanist insult for monks, suggesting their arguments were merely meaningless, repetitive croaking.</note>. I have set other machines in motion. Our cause is now conducted under the names of the Great of the Earth, of whom those wretched ones are most afraid." †)

"If Germany will listen to me," Ulrich von Hutten writes to the Count of Neuenar in April 1518, "we must wage war against the monks sooner than against the Turks. For what does the downfall of the Ottomans help us if we continue to tolerate in our midst those perverters of true piety, those defilers of the Christian religion, those authors of schisms and disputes, and those enemies of the sciences? To further the acceptance of the sciences, it is not enough to merely despise these people! No! The barbarians must be completely driven out, and only the true scholars must be generally respected. We have, to be sure, made a beginning in this, but the matter is not yet..."

Those who possess the confidence of the Emperor, Ulrich von Hutten wrote in November of that same year to Conrad Peutinger <note>Conrad Peutinger (1465–1547) was a prominent humanist, jurist, and diplomat in Augsburg.</note>, “seem to defer greatly to our faction.” <note>original Latin: "Hi factioni nostræ plurimum deferre videntur."</note> The highly influential advisors of other princes, and the princes themselves, promise us the same. We call them <term>Maecenates and Augusti: These are references to Gaius Maecenas (a famous Roman patron of the arts) and Emperor Augustus; Hutten uses them as titles for wealthy patrons of learning.</term> not because they already deserve these titles of honor, but to encourage them to emulate great models. We have indeed already forced several, as if by shame, to come over to our side, and have instilled in them the opinion that it is worthy of a prince to favor the sciences and humanities. Therefore, my advice is to set nets for this class of men everywhere and to obtain their favor in every permissible way, etc. <note>original Latin: "Aliquos jam enim coëgimus pudore sui benefacere nobis... favori principum retia tendere &c." Hutten is describing a strategic "PR campaign" to shame or entice nobility into supporting the humanist cause.</note>

"Take the rope, you theologians," <note>An idiom essentially telling them to hang themselves in shame or surrender.</note> says the same great defender of truth and freedom in the postscript to the *Triumph of Capnio* <term>Triumphus Capnionis: A satirical poem by Hutten celebrating Reuchlin’s victory. Much is being drawn forth from Greek and Hebrew. The great work is being pursued with vigor. And what do you do in the meantime? This: that you rob our times and the sciences of Reuchlin! > I did not name all those who appear in my list merely to honor them. I know very well that in this list, the learned and unlearned, the good and the bad, even friends and enemies are mixed together. The learned and the good were worthy of praise; the good and the powerful—even if they were not very enlightened—were intended to be set up as a defensive wall against the wicked. The scholars who were either doubtful or even unfavorably disposed, I wanted to encourage and win over, and to instill suspicion in our adversaries against other adversaries. My expectations were not disappointed. I have caused much greater movements than I myself had hoped. I have not only strengthened the wavering but have mostly brought them over to our side; and several of the greatest patrons of our enemies I have made suspicious or hateful to their own party. Even the most holy men suppress the indignation which my praise has aroused in them, not out of love for me, but because they know that I can both help and harm them.

...the *Parts of Alexander* <note>original: "partes Alexandri"; a standard medieval grammar textbook by Alexander de Villa Dei</note>, or the *Vade Mecum* <note>original: "vade mecum"; meaning "Go with me," a portable handbook</note>, or the *Exercise of Boys* <note>original: "exercitium puerorum"</note>, or the *Lesser Work* <note>original: "opus minus"</note>, or the sayings used by **Johann Sinthen** <note>A prominent 14th-century grammarian</note>. The **Masters of Arts** were held in great honor, and when students saw one of them, they were as terrified as if the devil himself had appeared to them. Degrees were conferred four times each year, and every time no fewer than fifty to sixty **Bachelors** were made. During this golden age of the university, young people were elevated to the dignity of **Bachelor** in a year and a half, and to the **Master’s degree** in two and a half or three years. Parents gladly spent the money for their sons because they saw that their children soon became something of status. 

Now, however, the youth wish to hear **Virgil**, **Pliny**, and other new authors; and even if they have listened to these for five years, they still do not ask to be granted a degree. — In his time, the Master continued, there were surely two thousand students in **Leipzig**, just as many in **Erfurt**, four thousand in **Vienna**, as many in **Cologne**, and so on. Now, in all of them combined, there are not as many as there formerly were in one or two, because the **Poets** <note>The "Poets" was a derogatory term used by traditionalists for the Humanist scholars who focused on classical literature</note> do them the greatest harm. 

When parents, the Master further complained, still send their children to the **bursaries** <note>original: "Bursen"; communal student hostels</note> and colleges, the boys no longer want to stay, but instead go to the poets and listen to all sorts of follies. He himself once had forty students under his supervision. These all followed behind him whenever he visited the church, the bathhouse, or the **Rosenthal** <note>A famous park in Leipzig</note>. In those days, it was considered a great sin if someone occupied themselves with the art of poetry. If someone confessed in the confessional that he had heard **Virgil** from a **Bachelor**...

Would to God that things still stood this way at the high schools! Then I would no longer let myself be badgered here at the Roman court. 

But what are we to do now at the universities, where there are no longer any prospects for us? The young people no longer want to be in the bursaries or under the supervision of Masters. Among twenty students, hardly one seeks a degree. All want to study the ancient languages and writers. The **Masters** have no more listeners, and the students flock to the **Poets** in whole crowds. Thus, all the high schools throughout all of Germany are going to ruin. We must therefore pray to God that all poets perish. For it is better that one should die, than etc. <note>A dark parody of the biblical verse John 11:50, "It is better that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation perish"</note>

The Inquisition trial that Hogstraten now began against Reuchlin was in itself not only highly unjust but even directly contrary to the statutes of the Dominican Order. According to the statutes of his order, Hogstraten could not proceed as an Inquisitor against Reuchlin or any other defendant in a foreign province. Even if his provincial superior had authorized him to do so, Hogstraten still should not have accepted the commission, because according to the Dominican statutes, no Inquisitor was allowed to judge anywhere where he could not also preach; and Hogstraten could not do this in Mainz, as he was a Netherlander. Furthermore, Hogstraten did not accuse Reuchlin of <term>heresy</term> <note>Ketzerey</note>, but only of such assertions that "smacked of heresy"; and for the sake of such assertions, Hogstraten as an Inquisitor had no right to act as he actually did **). The court then scheduled the examination of witnesses for the following morning, declared the case closed in the afternoon, and set the next court date as the final deadline for the execution of the sentence. As the Chapter noticed that Hoogstraten did not wish to be reconciled and was intentionally dragging out the negotiations so that he could publicly burn the <term>Augenspiegel</term> <note>Reuchlin's 1511 work "The Eye-Glass," which defended the preservation of Jewish books.</note> once the deadline had expired, they dispatched a messenger on October 11—the final day of the granted grace period—to the Elector in Aschaffenburg. They requested that he command his advisors, who were members of the inquisitorial court, to suspend the passing and execution of the sentence against Reuchlin for another month, so that the matter might be settled amicably if possible. Hoogstraten learned nothing of this mission, and the Chapter itself was uncertain how its request would be received by the Archbishop, despite the fact that this lord was otherwise a fair-minded prince and experienced in matters of law. The twelfth of October, the terrible day of judgment, arrived. At eight o’clock, Hoogstraten and the other inquisitors emerged with solemn pomp and a numerous entourage of doctors from Mainz, Cologne, Leuven, and Erfurt, and proudly took their seats on the judicial benches. They were surrounded by a large crowd of people, some curious and others overly pious, because the Dominicans had promised three hundred days of indulgence to all those who would be present for the announcement and execution of the sentence as an "act of faith" <note>This refers to an *auto-da-fé*, a public ceremony of penance and punishment during the Inquisition.</note>. However, in order not to appear defeated, Hoogstraten announced an appeal to the papal see before a <term>Notarius</term> <note>A legal notary.</note> and witnesses to the Archbishop of Mainz, and had this very same appeal posted on the doors of the cathedral in Mainz. It contained statements that were as untrue as they were insolent: that the Elector had, in an unlawful manner to the great detriment of God's Church and to the significant scandal of the faithful, hindered the course of justice and abolished the inquisitorial court ***). After a consultation held with many legal scholars, Hoogstraten withdrew the <term>Appellation</term> <note>The formal legal appeal.</note> to the papal see, and neither he nor his clients had the heart to accept the invitation to a public disputation regarding Reuchlin’s case.

**Reuchlin** now began to realize that it was beneath his dignity and beyond his strength to personally counter every attack and insult from his countless and irrepressible opponents \*). He despised everything that was spoken, written, and printed against him. His friends, however, continued not only to publicly undertake his defense but also to attack his opponents, hoping they might finally force them into silence. These hopes were indeed frustrated. Nevertheless, no other defensive or polemical writing by **Reuchlin** and his friends struck the Cologne group and their followers so low as the *Letters of Obscure Men* <note>original: "Epistolæ obscurorum virorum"</note>, the first part of which appeared at the beginning of the year 1517, followed shortly thereafter by the second part under the title *Letters of Famous Men* <note>original: "Epistolæ clarorum virorum"</note> \*\*). A more successful and effective parody and lampoon of ridiculous and contemptible men has never been written; never had the customs, the ignorance, and the corrupted language of the scholastic scholars and monks been depicted as truthfully and comically as in these letters. <page-num>192</page-num>

in the age in which they appeared, that hardly any other work did so much damage to the whole **Papacy** as this remarkable product of **German wit** \*). The monks themselves soon realized that the letters written in their names would inflict incurable wounds upon them if they remained in the public’s hands for long. They therefore purchased, as soon as possible and for a great sum of money, a **Papal Brief** <term>päpstliches Breve; a formal decree from the Pope</term> which threatened anyone who read the *Letters of Obscure Men* or failed to burn them after the announcement of the Papal will with the penalty of **excommunication** <term>Bann; exclusion from the church and sacraments</term>. This was a penalty that only the Pope himself could lift, and only in the hour of death \*\*). To force the monks to once again incur the costs of purchasing such a Brief, **Pirkheimer** <note>Willibald Pirkheimer (1470–1530), a prominent German humanist and lawyer</note> advised his friend **Hutten** <note>Ulrich von Hutten (1488–1523), a knight and humanist satirist</note> that they must print the second part under the title *Letters of Illustrious Men* (*Epistolæ clarorum virorum*) †). Reuchlin's friends gave him great hope for a swift and happy outcome from the beginning of the year 1515, when his case truly began to move in Rome, and for a long time thereafter \*). From the very start in Rome, the main question was this: Did Reuchlin's **Augenspiegel** <note>literally "Eyeglass"; Reuchlin’s 1511 defense against accusations of heresy regarding Jewish books</note> contain such propositions as **Hoogstraten** alleged, or was this writing as harmless and even useful as it had been declared in the final judgment of the commissioners at **Speyer**? To justify his opinion and that of his followers, **Hoogstraten** submitted a translation of Reuchlin’s *Augenspiegel* which was provided with a seal from the **University of Cologne**, or at least from the theological faculty of that high school. Reuchlin's procurator <note>a legal representative in the Roman courts</note>, on the other hand, maintained that this translation was incomplete and in many places intentionally falsified. The Papal commissioners therefore ordered that sworn translators of Reuchlin's *Augenspiegel* be appointed by both sides, and that their translations thereafter be examined by impartial men experienced in both the Roman <note>Latin</note> and German languages. On Reuchlin's side, a Doctor **Martin Gröning** from Bremen, who happened to be present in Rome, took over the translation of Reuchlin's work into Latin. The translator for the opposing party remains unknown. As both translations were

The wickedness of these abominable people has not merely left an eternal stain on the city of Rome and the memory of **Leo X.** <note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521), who initially viewed the Lutheran dispute as a minor "monk's quarrel."</note>, nor merely drawn the most intense hatred of all European peoples upon the entire order, but it has also forced almost every well-meaning and enlightened man to go over to **Luther's** party, which they have begun to ignite like a new blaze.

until it took hold of the very peaks of the church building.

The **mendicant monks** <note>Religious orders such as the Dominicans and Franciscans who took vows of poverty; here the author views them as power-hungry.</note> took the same path, and met the same end, that the **Jesuits** and indeed the practitioners of every illegitimate power later took and met. They achieved their power through the ignorance of all other social classes and through intrigues that were highly effective among unenlightened peoples—but only among such people. They sought to increase and solidify the power they had gained not through true merit, but through the same dark arts by which it had been founded. 

The arrogance and violence of the mendicant monks, combined with their highly corrupt morals and a gross ignorance, gradually gave rise to a dangerous envy, hatred, and even contempt. Instead of softening these sentiments through a sincere improvement of their lives, they only inflamed them further through the injustice with which they suppressed their first adversaries—who loudly defended truth, virtue, and religion against the protectors of ignorance, superstition, and vice. 

With the ever-increasing hatred and contempt, their enemies multiplied. Every new struggle became more difficult because the unjust weapons they had used until then—overt violence, slanders, and other intrigues—lost their effectiveness. The mendicant monks paid no heed to any of this, because they considered themselves invincible, or the highest spiritual nobility, whom the head of the church must not abandon even when they were in the wrong. In this delirium of invincibility, they not only failed to moderate or change their behavior, but they

# Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim.

Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim <note>Agrippa (1486–1535) was a polymath, physician, and legal scholar, best known today for his work on "occult philosophy" or magic.</note> did not have nearly the influence on his own and subsequent ages that **Reuchlin** <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note> or the greatest among the reformers living at that time possessed. Nevertheless, Agrippa deserves to be counted among the most remarkable scholars of the first half of the sixteenth <unclear>century</unclear> because of the adventurous nature of his genius, his character, and his fate; because of the connections he established and in which he lived; because of the feuds he waged; because of the secret arts <term>secret arts: refers to occultism, alchemy, and Hermetic philosophy</term> which he taught and practiced; and because of the extraordinary admiration and enmity with which some idolized him and others persecuted him.

The preparations for the biography which I will now present to my readers have convinced me anew that one cannot provide a truly satisfying and instructive life description of a <unclear>scholar</unclear> unless one has read all of his works with attention and, in doing so, has carefully noted: In which times and situations each individual work was writ—

...was written: when, in what locations, and with what level of acclaim a person taught; how the writer and teacher had a beneficial or detrimental effect on his contemporaries, and was in turn shaped, or misshaped, by those same contemporaries; which and how many friends or enemies he acquired or attracted; and whether the value and reputation of his writings were fleeting or lasting? — Among all the biographers of Agrippa, there is not one who has sufficiently satisfied these fair requirements. **Bayle** is by far the most complete and precise in the article of his dictionary <note>Pierre Bayle’s *Dictionaire Historique et Critique*, a massive biographical encyclopedia from the late 17th century.</note> that deals with Agrippa. ## Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
was born in the year 1487 *) in Cologne <note>original: "Cölln"</note> from an ancient, wealthy family of tournament-eligible rank <note>term: "turnierfähig" — referring to the high noble status required to participate in knightly tournaments.</note>, which had for a long time dedicated itself to the service of the House of Austria **). From his—

<margin>
*) Bayle sets Agrippa's birthday as September 14, 1486, without proof. The following words of Agrippa prove that he was born in 1487. Vol II. p. 595. 596 of the *Works in Defense of Propositions*: "For in the year of human salvation one thousand five hundred and nine, in the twenty-second year of my age..." <note>original: "II. 595. 596. Oper. in Def. Propos. Nam anno humanæ salutis millesimo quingentesimo nono ætatis meæ vicesimo secundo - - -"</note>

**) I infer the tournament-eligibility of Agrippa’s family from the following passage in the *Preface to the Book on the Vanity of the Sciences*: "Nobles in purple will remove (me). Heralds in military cloaks will strip away the images of my ancestors, and in the ordained equestrian games, which they call tournaments, they will cry out against me as a rustic tax-collector." <note>original: "Submovebunt (me) purpurati nobiles. Exuent majorum imagines paludati Heraldi, indictisque equitiis, quæ torneamenta vocant, pro rustico exactionario inclamitabunt."</note> That his family was old, wealthy, and very devoted to the House of Austria is stated by Agrippa in several places: *Book VI. Letter 18*: "Furthermore, both my father, and grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, and great-great-grandfathers were for a long age ministers of the Roman Emperors and Austrian princes." <note>original: "Proinde et pater, et avi, et atavi, et tritavi Cæsarum Romanorum, Austriacorumque principum a longo ævo ministri fuerunt."</note> and *VII. 21. Ep.*: "My ancestors, always devoted to the Austrian princes from the time of my grandfathers and great-grandfathers, brought back distinguished marks of their virtues and fortunes." <note>original: "Majores mei ab avis et atavis Austriacis principibus semper addicti, virtutum suarum præclara insignia fortunasque reportarunt."</note> In many places, but especially in the letter to the Council of Cologne, he calls this city his fatherland. *VII. Letter 26. p. 1041*: "For I am, if perhaps you do not know, sprung from your city, and nourished among you in my earliest childhood." <note>original: "Sum enim et ego, si forte nescitis, civitate vestra oriundus, et prima pueritia apud vos enutritus."</note> Schelhorn and Rave concluded from the following words of a friend that Agrippa’s family originated from the Netherlands. *Letter V. 15*: "Nor do I see a reason why you would prefer to remain in Gallic Lyon <note>original: "Gallia Lugdunensi"</note> rather than your Belgium <note>original: "tua Belgica"</note>, which produced you." An even more apparent proof could have been found in a letter which Agrippa wrote on the journey from Lyon to Antwerp, in which he says: "for I am migrating back to my fatherland" <note>original: "remigro enim in patriam"</note> *V. 21. Letters*. However, I do not believe that Agrippa’s ancestors had moved from the Netherlands to Cologne within human memory. Agrippa would certainly not have forgotten this circumstance in the letters he wrote to the councilors of the Emperor and to the two regents of the Netherlands, Margaret and Mary. Agrippa's friend called Lower Germany on the other side of the Rhine, which did not belong to the French, "Belgic Gaul" <note>original: "Gallia Belgica"</note> after the ancient manner, and Agrippa saw the Netherlands as a part of Germany.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim, following his departure from Germany. It describes his return to Paris and his involvement in a dangerous political and military scheme in the Pyrenees.</meta>

<page-num>218</page-num>

Nothing prevented Agrippa, toward the end of the year 1507 or at the beginning of the following year, from reuniting with his brothers <note>The "brothers" refers to the secret society of scholars and mystics Agrippa had helped form.</note> in Paris. Not long after his arrival in the French capital, our Agrippa was drawn into an undertaking that seemed questionable to him from the very start. This was caused by the reckless praises that one of his friends, Galbianus, had bestowed upon him in the presence of a courtier, and by the extraordinary expectations that the repetition of these praises had stirred in the King. The project went against his principles and against the agreements made with his friends; however, for a short time, it held great appeal for him because of the significant rewards promised for a successful outcome \*). Soon afterward, it appeared so dangerous to him that he was on the verge of deciding to flee in secret to avoid being forced to fulfill the promises made by his friends \*\*). Finally, against his own inclination and conviction, Agrippa threw himself into a plan that became a source of unspeakable anxieties and dangers for him for an entire year. It revealed him to his contemporaries and to posterity in all his adventurousness, for the young man risked his conscience, his good name, his freedom, and his life merely to reach a state of brilliant fortune through one desperate stroke. The plan consisted of seizing a fortified castle called the **Black Castle** <note>original: "schwarze Burg"</note>, located in the **Round Valley** <note>original: "runden Thale"</note> not far from the foot of the eastern Pyrenees, from the hands of rebellious peasants, and returning it to the King through the arts or stratagems of Agrippa.

\*) Book I, Letter 4.
\*\*) Book I, Letter 5.

<page-num>219</page-num>

A friend and brother of the order to which Agrippa belonged, **Jeannot** or **Jeanotte** \*\*), had been the commander of this castle. He had so greatly violated the freedoms of the neighboring country folk, or perhaps practiced such harsh extortions, that all the inhabitants of the surrounding areas revolted, drove the commander out, and occupied the captured fortress as a bulwark of their freedom. Agrippa himself recognized that the reconquest of the Black Castle was not only a foolhardy but also a cruel undertaking, through which one might at best please the incensed King, but would, on the other hand, make oneself hated by all other people and even by many nobles at court. These latter figures had already described him to the King as an extremely dangerous man \*\*\*). As often as Agrippa reflected on all of this himself, and as strongly as he had presented it to his friends, he nevertheless allowed himself to be led by them into a hateful plan, through which Jeannot hoped to regain the King's favor at Agrippa's expense and risk. The undertaking actually succeeded. By all appearances, the Black Castle was conquered through treachery,

When the peasants learned that the castle's garrison had saved themselves in the tower, they sought to storm it immediately. However, because they did not have even small firearms, much less heavy artillery, but only crossbows and arrows, and the besieged fired out from behind their breastworks, they soon gave up the assault and decided to force their enemies to surrender by siege and starvation. During this siege of the tower, the Abbot of the neighboring monastery, who was held in great esteem throughout the region, took every conceivable pain to pacify the country folk and persuade them to an acceptable peace. But the besiegers replied: That they had not rebelled against the King, but against the tyranny of Jeannot and his accomplices, who had taken away their old freedom under the pretext of royal protection and had practiced unheard-of cruelties and extortions against them: That they would therefore not rest until they had seized the German <note>meaning Agrippa himself</note>, as well as Jeannot, so that these men could not provoke the King against them anew and plunge them once more into ruin \*\*).

This discovery, though little comforting, prompted a plan in a general council held by the distressed: That the Abbot must be notified and asked to secretly send a ship to the rock where Perotte had descended, in order to cross the lake from there. to give news to the Abbot was almost impossible, because the peasants held all exits of the tower, and of the entire valley in which the tower lay, with the greatest care; they would almost certainly have captured anyone who attempted to sneak through their guards. Without the cunning of the adventurous Agrippa, the besieged would hardly have succeeded in informing the Abbot of their situation and the only means of their rescue. Agrippa smeared the hands and face of a shepherd boy, who belonged to the tower-keeper, with all kinds of herbs to make it look as if he had leprosy <note>Leprosy was a feared and highly contagious disease in the Middle Ages; sufferers were socially exiled.</note>. On the following morning, the supposedly leprous shepherd boy began to beg with a stammering voice in the peasants' camp. Wherever he turned, people fled from him as if from a deadly plague, throwing him alms from a great distance. Begging his way, the boy arrived undetected at the Abbey, and returned the next day with the Abbot’s answer: that the Abbot would send two boats <note>original: "Nachen" — small, flat-bottomed rowing boats</note> with red pennants the following day to pick up the fugitives. In this manner, Agrippa and his companions escaped an obvious danger of death and arrived safely at the Abbey, where they rested for some time from their tribulations. The Abbot tried to persuade Agrippa to return to the Court and test the King’s favor once more. However much Agrippa was tempted by the proposal, he nevertheless resisted the lures of fortune this time. He feared that the King

would immediately want to use him for a new and dangerous undertaking. But it seemed even more dubious to him to entrust himself and his entire welfare to unknown people, as all his friends were absent from the Court. While he was still uncertain what he should begin, he met an old wandering adventurer in the Abbey by the name of Antonius Xanthus. Though Xanthus possessed no scholarly knowledge, he had traveled extensively and was faithful and discreet. This man simultaneously determined, strengthened, and steadied the wavering and wandering mind of Agrippa, who otherwise might have blindly abandoned himself to fate without specific goals, or, in the truest sense, gone out seeking adventure to visit unknown peoples and lands \*). The old man advised him to go first to Spain, and from there to Italy, because one might perhaps receive news of Landulph <note>Landulph was one of Agrippa’s closest associates and a member of his secret philosophical circle.</note> there. At the same time, he offered to accompany Agrippa and to share both fortune and danger with him. The experience of this old man was so instructive for Agrippa, and his company so comforting, that he soon admitted him into the secret bond or order which he had founded with his friends in Paris \*\*). Thus, along with another friend named *Stephanus*, *Agrippa* traveled in September 1508 to *Barcelona*, and from there to *Valencia*, where they inquired after *Landulph* with the *Saracen Lamparatus*, a famous *astrologer* and student of *Jacutus*. Since they heard nothing of their fellow brother <term>Ordensbruder: a member of Agrippa's secret society dedicated to the occult and mutual support</term> there, they sold their horses and set sail for *Naples*. In this city, the travelers did not find the fortune they had expected, and they therefore decided to return to *France*. Toward the end of the year 1508, *Agrippa* and his companions went ashore in *Provence* and remained stranded in *Avignon* because their travel funds had run out. The adversities that *Agrippa* had endured, and the failed attempts he had made in *Spain* and *Italy* with his secret arts, did not produce in him the slightest change of heart, nor even the thought: whether it might not perhaps be more advisable to seek fortune through the path of truth, prudence, and virtue with the gifts and knowledge he possessed, rather than, as before, through deception and cunning. As soon as he arrived in *Avignon*, he set up his *gold-making shop* <note>original: "Goldmacherbude" — a disparaging or cynical term for an alchemical laboratory</note>, as he expressed it himself, in order to scrape together money for the further journey *): And since he learned shortly thereafter that *Landulph* was in *Lyon*, nothing was more urgent to him than the renewal of the covenant that had been scattered for a time, and the summoning or notification of the members, to whom various provin-

The brothers of the order were delighted almost to the point of madness by the news of *Agrippa’s* rescue and his fortunate arrival in France; most of all *Landulph*, who had sought *Agrippa* throughout all of *Navarre*, *Gascony*, and the rest of southern France **). His lectures were so well-received by high-ranking officials and scholars that he was granted a salaried professorship at the University of Dole at the age of twenty-two.</summary>

The eloquence and scholarship with which Agrippa interpreted Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew whose work on the Kabbalah deeply influenced Agrippa.</note> necessarily increased his reputation for magic and his magical practice, toward which his present as well as absent brothers of the order continued to contribute most powerfully.

"The bearer of this," wrote an absent friend to Agrippa around the same time †), "is the servant of a prominent French nobleman who needs your advice and help. The man is rich and generous. I have secured this opportunity for profit for you. Yet I seek to provide not merely for your benefit, but also for your honor. Therefore, come if you can appear with a certain splendor. You know how much prestige and weight lies in a fine garment, especially among those fools who look only at the outward appearance of a person. If you cannot show yourself with a certain dignity, then excuse yourself and postpone your journey until I can come to your aid. Should the nobleman surprise you in Dole, then do and promise nothing except after long entreaties and great rewards. Even if you are quite poor, let nothing of it be noticed. The man is eager. One must strike the iron while it is hot. Look after your fortune: I shall not fail to promote it as much as I can." The primary intention why Agrippa appeared as a teacher in Dole was this: that he wished to recommend himself to Princess Margaret <note>Margaret of Austria (1480–1530), daughter of Emperor Maximilian I and Regent of the Netherlands.</note>, Regent of the Netherlands; for which reason he also says that he lectured on

...the location and time of the creation of woman, from the material out of which *Eve* was formed, from religion, reason, history, and experience, and from divine and human laws. The name of the first man, says *Agrippa*, means merely "earth," and the name of the first woman means "life"; and this very name has much more similarity to the ineffable name of divine omnipotence <note>The Tetragrammaton, or the four-letter name of God in Hebrew.</note>—of which *Reuchlin* treats in his book *On the Wonder-Working Word* <note>original: "de verbo mirifico"</note>—than the name *Adam* \*). In the creation of the world, God always proceeded from the less good and noble toward the more excellent and noble. The first man was created after the animals, and the woman was created after the man. God created *Adam*, like the rest of the livestock, outside of Paradise; *Eve*, however, was created within Paradise itself: *Adam* from mere earth, but *Eve* from a part of the first-created human. For this reason, woman is much more beautiful and perfect than man \*\*); and as a more sublime being, a woman never feels vertigo, as a man does, when she looks down into the depths from steep heights †). Even in the fluids which cleansing nature separates at certain times <note>A reference to menstrual blood, which in the Renaissance was often believed to possess potent magical or medicinal properties.</note>, there lie wonderful powers, the likes of which are not found in the body of man ††). Holy Scripture, *Agrippa* further declaims, everywhere gives preference to the woman over the man. The latter sinned knowingly; the former was merely seduced. God blessed the man

*Agrippa's* speech did not have the effect that he and his friends had promised themselves. The cause of the young orator’s thwarted prospects was the Provincial of the Franciscans, *Jean Catilinet* <note>original: "Johann Catiliner"</note>, who in the year 1510 held the Lenten sermons before the court of Princess *Margaret* in *Ghent*. Among other insults which he poured out, he called *Agrippa* a "judaizing heretic" who wished to introduce the *Kabbalah* and the *Talmud* into the Christian religion †). Before *Agrippa* even learned the consequences of these slanders, one of his most venerable patrons and friends, *Theodoric*, Bishop of *Cyrene*, invited him (and through him, his parents) to return to *Cologne*...

From Cologne, he visited the famous Abbot Tritheim in Würzburg, stayed for a time in his monastery, and conversed with him about chemical, magical, cabbalistic, and other secret arts and sciences. Together with this admirer of the secret arts, he especially investigated the question: how it came to pass that Magic and Cabbala, which were regarded by the sages and priests of the most ancient times as the most sublime of all sciences, were always disdained and condemned by the fathers and teachers of the Christian Church **)? Agrippa departed from Abbot Tritheim with the greatest reverence for this adept, and with strengthened zeal for the secret sciences, to which he had been devoted since his early youth, and returned to Cologne. His spirit was, as he himself says, awakened within him, and at the encouragement of Tritheim, he wrote his three books *De occulta philosophia* <note>original: "On Occult Philosophy"</note>, in order to restore ancient and high magic to its former purity; to cleanse it of all the dross by which it had been defiled; and finally to defend it against the reproaches of dangerous heresies, through which it had been made suspicious †). But after our conversation in Würzburg <note>Latin: *Herbipoli*</note> on these matters, your excellent skill and learning, and your ardent exhortation, gave me the audacity and the courage."

What raised him from his sad situation was the hope, which had already been thwarted once, of winning the favor of the **Marquess of Montferrat** <note>The Marquisate of Montferrat was a sovereign state in Northern Italy; Agrippa frequently sought patronage from its rulers.</note>, and obtaining from him an office or at least a pension. He therefore dedicated to this gentleman in the year 1516 first his dialogue *On Man* <note>original: "de homine"</note>, which was never printed, and then his small treatise *On the Knowledge of God* <note>original: "de Dei notitia"</note> \*), or *On the Threefold Way of Knowing God* <note>original: "de triplici ratione cognoscendi deum"</note> \*\*), which is composed entirely in the spirit of the mystical theologians or the theological mages.

**Agrippa** used mystical <term>theology</term> <note>The study of God through direct experience or intuition rather than just rational debate.</note>, like <term>alchemy</term> and other secret arts, as lures for others who were more serious about them than he was himself. And yet, one would do him an injustice to believe that he had constantly been nothing more than a fraud, and that he merely pretended to believe in <term>alchemy</term> and higher <term>theology</term>—which he secretly despised—solely to deceive others. **Agrippa** never ceased to believe in the reality of secret arts, even when he mocked them or knowingly stirred up expectations in others that he could not fulfill. In the same way, at least between the years 1515 and 1520, he was a true

The true piety, wisdom, and happiness of man, says **Agrippa** \*), consists in the knowledge and love of God. In this mystical declamation, Agrippa asserted—as many others before him had already suspected—that the Fall of Man was nothing more than the first illicit enjoyment of sensual love, and that the serpent had been the procreative member of the first human ***): That original sin, therefore, consists in the sensuality or "lust of the flesh" arising from that first fall. In Agrippa's opinion, the first parents lived in virginal purity and abstinence before the Fall, and marriage only arose once Adam and Eve had made themselves unworthy of Paradise. If the inhabitants of Paradise had not been overcome by the temptations of their flesh, then humans—as he had proven more extensively in his writing *On Man* <note>original: *de homine*</note>—would have been propagated in the state of innocence by a seed other than the carnal one †). <meta>This page continues the biography of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa during his time in Metz (c. 1518-1519), moving from his mystical interpretations of original sin to his growing conflict with the monastic orders over humanism and Church authority.</meta>

<page-num>256</page-num>
<meta>catchword: enchanting</meta>

Approximately around the same time that he composed his discourse on original sin, or perhaps slightly earlier, Agrippa wrote the *Exhortation against Pagan Theology* <note>original: *dehortatio gentilis theologiæ*</note> for the instruction of several friends. These friends had requested from him an interpretation of the book *On the Power of God* <note>A text from the *Corpus Hermeticum*, then attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note>, which had been falsely attributed to Hermes; in response, he had offered them an interpretation of the Pauline Epistles instead *). In this warning, Agrippa cautions his friends against a too-diligent study of the writings of Hermes, Plato, Plotinus, and others. They might, he said, certainly form their writing style and their spirit through the words of these men; however, it was much safer to stick to the sole source of unadulterated truth: the Holy Scriptures. Anyone who, alongside the Scriptures, also studied the pagan philosophers with great effort and loss of time, acted like a sick man who had an experienced, skillful, and honest physician, yet still took refuge with quacks who could not help him. In the writings of the pagan philosophers, error and truth were mixed together. Through these errors, the mind can easily be twisted and made less receptive to the pure truths of the holy books. — These judgments lasted in Agrippa just as briefly as those concerning the vanity of all profane sciences, and even the secret sciences.

Whenever Agrippa spoke around this time about the importance of the holy scriptures and teachings, he did so with an irresistible, or rather enchant—

Agrippa countered his opponent's positions with his own *Conclusions*, which he likewise shared with Faber in Paris *). Faber, a lover of truth but also a man of peace who was convinced of the inherent power of truth, repeatedly begged Agrippa **): that he should not get involved in any dispute with the ignorant and slanderous monks. Such a struggle would bring him no honor and the truth no advantage, for truth would gradually triumph on its own, and false delusions would sink away by themselves. Agrippa did not follow this advice. To this was added the fact that the corrupt monk had accepted gifts from the defendant's enemies, that he had usurped an unauthorized jurisdiction contrary to all laws, that he had moved the legal proceedings away from the proper "jurisdiction" <note>original: *Foro*; the appropriate legal venue</note> or place of the court, and that he had set himself up as a judge while being completely inexperienced in the law. This trial was so unjust and revolting that the Cathedral Chapter in *Metz* gave the order to return the prisoner to the city. ...had allowed himself to be led by the greedy witch-hunter <note>original: "Ketzermeister," literally a master of heretics or grand inquisitor</note>, he became terminally ill immediately afterward. Tormented by pangs of conscience on his deathbed, he made a confession before a notary and witnesses, which was then presented to the Cathedral Chapter: that the defendant was innocent, and even if she had made herself suspicious, she had been sufficiently purified and punished by the torture she had already endured. The Inquisitor *Savini* did not allow himself to be appeased even by this incident. Rather, with inhuman shamelessness, he demanded that the prisoner be tortured anew and then handed over to the stake. The primary reason for this petition was the superstition drawn from the *Malleus Maleficarum* <note>The *Hammer of Witches*, a 1486 treatise on the prosecution of witches</note>: that the mother of the defendant had been burned as a witch; and that witches usually dedicated their children to the devil from birth—indeed, that they mostly conceived their children from the devil himself. *Agrippa* replied that these assertions were heresies that were equal to those of *Faustus* and *Donatus* <note>Faustus of Riez and Donatus were leaders of early Christian sects deemed heretical for their views on grace and the sacraments</note>: that by such claims, the power of baptism was entirely nullified. He argued that even if one admitted that devils could procreate, no man had ever believed that devils—besides the seed stolen from other men—could produce such a thing of their own accord <note>Agrippa is referencing the scholastic theory that demons (incubi/succubi) could not generate life themselves but merely transported human seed</note>. Based on the defense which *Agrippa* presented before the successor of the first official, the prisoner was granted her freedom. The accusers were severely punished, and the Inquisitor was not only rejected in his petition but was generally despised and loathed. †)

Instead, he was driven away from *Freyburg*, as he had been from Metz, by his innate restlessness—a trait reinforced by the life he had led until then—by virtue of which his present circumstances never satisfied him for long, and the near future always appeared more brilliant to him than it did to other, more impartial observers. The actual occasions for his departure from *Freyburg*, however, were the proposals he received simultaneously from the Duke of *Bourbon* and from the French court. For a time, he was uncertain which he should accept; and it was even rumored that he had entered the service of the Duke of *Bourbon* as a captain †). Ultimately, however, he preferred the grand offers of the French court, and persuaded his two relatives...

In no other work did <term>Agrippa</term> show himself to be such a fine and bold thinker, such a shrewd observer, such a great scholar, and such a practiced orator as in the book <term>De vanitate scientiarum</term>; and this is all the more to be admired since he wrote the best of his works at a time when he suffered from a lack of everything; where he felt completely abandoned by those to whom he had sacrificed everything and from whom he had expected the highest fortune, and where he was not infrequently near the most comfortless despair. This situation made him dissatisfied with the whole world—especially with the classes of people whom he saw as the authors of his misfortune, and with the sciences which he was supposed to practice but did not want to, or which he gladly wanted to apply but could not. The bitterness of his soul revealed itself not merely in his letters <margin>*) See especially the highly bitter description of the mendicant monks in Book IV, Letter 32, and that of court life and courtiers in Book IV, Letters 54 and 62.</margin>, but also in the dedication and preface of the book itself, where he says that he will bite like a dog, or sting like a snake, or wound like a dragon <margin>**) <note>original Latin: "Ipsumque jacet ingenium fortunæ meæ indignatione dejectum, adeo ut ex ipsa indignatione ferme cum Trojana illa Hecuba versus sim in canem - - - - nil amplius memini, nisi mordere, oblatrare, maledicere, convitiari: - - - - verum ego nunc e cane in crocodilum, aut draconem, aliumve igneomum serpentem migrabo." — Translation: My very talent lies cast down by the indignation of my fate, so much so that from this indignation I am turned, much like that Trojan Hecuba, into a dog... I remember nothing more than biting, barking, cursing, and reviling... but now I shall pass from being a dog into a crocodile, or a dragon, or some other fire-breathing serpent.</note></margin>. The same bitterness, mixed with pride, prevails in the motto or small poem about himself which Agrippa had printed before the dedication in the first edition of his book, and which was repeated in the subsequent editions of the same work. Agrippa would likely have expressed the resentment simmering within him differently than he did, had he not possessed both a habit for <term>declamations</term> <note>rhetorical exercises or speeches intended to provoke or entertain rather than state literal facts</note> strengthened by practice, and, at several points in his earlier life, strong bouts of a fanatical contempt for all worldly sciences or profane wisdom. From these present and former impressions and skills arose the rhetorical indictment of most arts, sciences, and social classes. For this very reason—because it was the result of purely fleeting states of mind—one cannot conclude Agrippa's true opinions from it at all: perhaps with the exception of those articles where he speaks of the failings of scholastic sciences, the abuses in religion, and the corruption of the clergy. Nevertheless, the book *On the Vanity of Sciences* belongs to those writings of the sixteenth century which caused the greatest sensation and which still deserve to be read today: especially by those who concern themselves with the history of the sciences, of customs, and of the prevailing

<page-num>291</page-num>

way of thinking in the first half of the sixteenth century. No judgment of Agrippa’s work is more lopsided, or betrays a greater ignorance of the circumstances under which it was written, than that which declared the declamation *On the Vanity of Sciences* to be a guide to or a recommendation of <term>Skepticism</term> <note>the philosophical position that one should suspend judgment because certainty is impossible</note>. Agrippa occasionally rejected the worldly sciences. He was at times indignant toward the secret arts. However, he was never a "doubter." Agrippa’s faith and reverence toward the Christian religion always remained unshaken; and these were almost the only things in which he never became inconsistent. One would have to admire his frankness, as well as his erudition, his sharp wit, and the power of his language, if he had not, carried away by his wrath, gone too far in his public censure of powerful classes and of abuses that were indeed ruinous, yet considered sacred. Since Agrippa’s writing is not rare, it would be impractical to provide a full excerpt from it. I shall, therefore, only highlight such passages that, in my judgment, characterize either the author or the age.

Among other mostly well-founded reproaches which Agrippa makes against history and historians in general, he also puts forward this: Historians recount much that is not useful, approve of much that they should blame, and present people and actions as worthy of imitation which they should actually abhor. When they, for example, exalt an *Alexander*, *Pompey*, *Caesar*, *Hannibal*, and other conquerors to the heavens; what is that but praising great and raging...
