<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author further explores Agrippa’s scathing critique of human knowledge, moving from a condemnation of military "glory" into the dangers of eloquence, sophistry, and the moral decline associated with certain arts.</meta>

...highwaymen and desolators of the earth <note>original Latin: "Quid nisi magnos et furiosos latrones, famososque orbis praedones descripserunt?" — "What have they described but great and furious robbers, and famous plunderers of the world?" chapter 6, 5.</note>? Let the mentioned warriors have been great generals! It is even more certain that they were destructive men who destroyed the happiness of entire countries and peoples.

In the following section, Agrippa excellently demonstrates the abuse that has been made of eloquence <term>Beredsamkeit: the art of persuasive oratory</term> in ancient and modern times. It was, he says, always not only the tool of greed, ambition, and the lust for power, but also of destructive heresies and unbelief. One need only pay attention to what is happening in our times. Are not the heads of the Germanic sects and heresies, which were started by Luther and have so multiplied that almost every city has its own sect—are they not all great orators and writers, who were so praised a few years ago for their eloquence and elegant style of writing that nothing could be added to their praise? Again, there are other friends of ancient and beautiful literature who become pagans by seeking to imitate Cicero, or fall into superstition and unbelief by occupying themselves more than they should with Plato and Aristotle. — That the most famous poets and friends of ancient literature so greatly favored the Reformation made ancient literature and scholarship in general somewhat suspicious for a time in the 16th century, just as philosophy has now become suspicious because the authors and promoters of the Revolution in France named some great "world-wise" men <term>Weltweise: an archaic German term for philosophers</term> as their leaders, or were themselves considered philosophers by others.

<column-break/>

The subtleties of the ancient sophists, it says in the ninth section on Sophistry <term>Sophistik: the use of clever but false arguments, especially for deceptive purposes</term>, are nothing at all when compared with the inventions of the moderns, which constitute the sole occupation of teachers and disciples in the schools. Modern sophistry seems to have no other purpose than to lead to error and, through incessant quarreling, to obscure or ruin the truth. It is nothing more than a whimsical obsession that does violence to language, which is not understood, and perverts the entire use of speech through false meanings of words. Its glory consists in vituperation and making noise. It does not seek to find the truth and victory through it, but strives only for shouting and strife; and he is the first who makes the greatest noise and shows the greatest insolence. — Agrippa calls the Lullian art <note>Lullian Art: A system of logic and mnemonics developed by Ramon Llull in the 13th century, intended to prove the truths of faith through reason. Agrippa argues it became a tool for shallow vanity.</note> a monstrous art which merely teaches how to make a dazzling display of genius and scholarship, and to prattle about everything with a great flood of words while saying nothing; however, he softens this criticism by declaring it an "extraordinarily artistic and elegant invention" <note>original Latin: "Hoc plus, quam eleganti artificio." chapter 9.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim’s "De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum" (On the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences). ...here intentionally wanted to deceive others, rather than having been deceived himself.

In the two sections dealing with astronomy and astrology *), one recognizes both the imperfection of the former and the great prestige of the latter in **Agrippa’s** time, as well as the extraordinary effort he devoted to both throughout his life, and the resentment he had now conceived against them. **Agrippa** cites a great number of Jewish and Arabic *astrologers*, whose names are now not only unknown, but whose writings have likely for the most part perished. I too, he says, learned this art as a boy from my parents; and after I had lost much time and labor in learning it, I finally realized that it consists of nothing but daydreams and fictions. I regret having studied it so long and diligently. If I could, I would erase its memory from my mind, and would certainly never seek it out again, if the pleas of the Great <note>Meaning high-ranking nobles or patrons</note>, who so often misuse great spirits for unworthy things, did not force me, and if my own profit did not advise me to occasionally use their folly and satisfy them with trifles, since they wish to be fed with trifles. — *Astrology* ruins true philosophy, medicine, the law, and *religion* to the detriment of the human race. If one is found to be unfit for this, he may buy his nobility, which, like any other commodity, is for sale; or he may flatter kings, or act as a pimp <note>original: "Kuppler"</note> and trade his wife or his daughters. Or he may seek to make himself beloved by illustrious women, or marry the illegitimate daughter of a prince. These are the paths and steps by which one most easily and quickly ascends to the nobility. — The origin and nature of the nobility can be seen even from their coats of arms and shields. Among the four-footed animals as well as among the birds, none are considered noble, or symbols of nobility, except for the predatory beasts and birds of prey: lions, tigers, bears, wolves, leopards, dragons, snakes, eagles, vultures, falcons, hawks, ravens, ostriches, or even invented monsters, such as harpies, griffins, and so forth. Even the trees, types of stone, and metals used in coats of arms were chosen not from among the useful, but from among the unusable. Among the trees, only the oak, the beech, the laurel, and the myrtle tree; among the stones the most precious, the diamond, and so forth; and among the metals, gold and silver are considered noble.”

[...sovereignty] which did not begin with parricide, treason, bad faith, cruelty, carnage, slaughter, and other horrendous crimes—the arts, I say, of nobility. Since such are the heads of it, we will easily be able to recognize what the rest of the members of that beast are like: all of them prone and practiced in violence, robbery, slaughter, hunting, lust, and every kind of luxury.

The chapters in which Agrippa deals with medicine <note>original: "Arzneykunde"</note> and its various branches \*) must convince everyone of the imperfection of this science at that time, and of the manifold, now unheard-of charlatanries of the physicians of the 16th century. “The greatest reputation,” says Agrippa, “is now gained by those physicians who recommend themselves through magnificent clothes, through many rings and precious stones, through a distant fatherland, through tedious travels, through a different religion—especially the Jewish or Mohammedan <note>In the 16th century, foreign or non-Christian physicians were often exoticized and perceived as having "secret" ancient knowledge.</note>—and combine with these an enormous shamelessness in the praise of their remedies and miracle cures. — So that such quacks <note>original: "Quacksalber"</note> can make themselves even more important, they observe times and hours most precisely, always dispense their medicines according to the instructions of the astrological almanac, and hang all kinds of amulets on the sick. — Simple and native remedies are completely neglected. To these, they prefer expensive foreign medicines, mixing the latter in such enormous numbers that the effects of one are canceled out by those of another, or no human ingenuity can foresee the effects that will arise from such a hideous mixture.”

<margin>\*\*) Chapter 90.</margin>
In his remarks on alchemy, Agrippa appears in his usual double-tongued or two-sided manner \*\*). He mocks the deceptions, the follies, and the misery of the alchemists; declares their alleged secrets to be nothing but trifles, and then adds: “It would be far too extensive to [recount] the supposed mysteries of these people...”

"...I will tell you in person. However, so that you do not misunderstand me, I inform you in advance that I have been driven about—sometimes by the labors of war, sometimes by court life, and by various adverse fates—and have been held too tightly to this world by the love for my dear wife, such that I have not been able to attain the exalted gifts of the immortal gods myself. At the time Agrippa wrote these letters, the Duke of Bourbon <note>Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, a military leader who defected from France to the Holy Roman Empire; his death in 1527 led to the Sack of Rome.</note> had remained before Rome, and with him, all of Agrippa’s hopes centered on that fallen hero were brought to ruin. Agrippa therefore eagerly seized every opportunity that promised him new prospects, and for this reason, he announced himself to the Augustinian in Antwerp with an unusual, forthcoming politeness and the most glittering promises. This time, Agrippa actually achieved his purpose. The <term>Doctor ab Aquapendente</term> <note>original: "Doctor of Aquapendente"; likely referring to a scholar or physician from the town of Acquapendente.</note> promised Agrippa a pleasant stay in Antwerp \*\*) <note>Ibid., Letter 17.</note>, and even persuaded another respected man to write to Agrippa in his own name, and in the name of Augustinus Furnarius of Genoa, who was settled in Antwerp †) <note>Ibid., Letter 15.</note>. Agrippa's household was completely shattered by the death of his wife and the infectious disease from which she had died. He sent the children with a maid to the house of a friend, who, however, soon dismissed them both because of the latter’s bad behavior. Although Agrippa had not left his wife's sickbed for a single moment, he remained free from the **pestilence** <note>The plague or a similar epidemic sweeping Antwerp at the time</note>, which still continued to rage, and in which he saved many people, or at least believed he saved them <gloss>**) Book V. 84. The troubles in which Agrippa became entangled during the latter half of this year were the greatest obstacle preventing him from complying with his friend in London.

The most restless of Agrippa’s creditors received an order from the Privy Council in Brussels around the middle of August, commanding him to take no action against Agrippa’s person for a period of fourteen days. Nevertheless, three days later, this man had his debtor thrown into prison; however, Agrippa was soon freed through the intercession of the Archbishop of Palermo. The government in Brussels recognized that Agrippa had been wronged and that the creditor was obligated to give him satisfaction. Yet, they were unwilling to snatch Agrippa from the persecutions of his creditor by a formal decree, nor would the Treasury in Brussels—which owed Agrippa nearly two years' worth of salary—agree to act as his guarantor *). Finally, Agrippa attempted a last resort. He wrote a respectful but dry letter to the Emperor himself, in which he begged his master that, even if he could not reward Agrippa’s merits, he might at least grant him his dismissal. He asked that the Emperor not misinterpret this step, to which he had been driven by despair **). This letter seems to have brought Agrippa some relief, either through the receipt of a portion of his back pay or through the protection granted to him against the persecutions of his <term>usurers<note>Moneylenders who charge interest, often used disparagingly here to describe his aggressive creditors.</note></term>.

---

*) Book VI, Letters 25, 26.
**) Ibid. Letter 27.

During these days of deepest misery, or shortly thereafter, Agrippa received two letters: one from a friend of astrology, the other from a friend of "higher wisdom" in general. A <term>Right Reverend Father<note>A formal title for a high-ranking member of the clergy.</note></term> asked Agrippa about the meaning of a comet that had recently appeared. In his reply, Agrippa first classifies comets according to the <term>planets<note>original: "Irrsternen," literally "wandering stars."</note></term> to which they belong, showing how many comets have been discovered so far as "servants" of each planet and what they have been named. Based on these classifications, he suspects that the current comet is either a Saturnian or a Mercurial comet. Agrippa states that a precise determination of its full significance would require so many investigations and calculations that he cannot perform them due to a lack of time and books. In general, however, one may assume that the body of the comet indicates the matter itself or the future event, while the tail indicates the regions where what the comet predicts will occur. Since the tail of this comet stretches directly toward the North, one must assume that the events it indicates or threatens will take place in the northern kingdoms *).

The friend of secret wisdom who turned to Agrippa was a French priest named Andreas **), who had left his homeland for the sole purpose of seeing the two great German sages, Erasmus and Agrippa—just as Pythagoras, Plato, and Apollonius had once traveled to Egypt, <term>Chaldea<note>An ancient region in Mesopotamia, often associated in the Renaissance with the origins of magic and astrology.</note></term>

...India, and so forth, in order to visit the Sages of the Orient †). This unnamed traveler first came to *Erasmus* <note>Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536), the most famous humanist scholar of the Northern Renaissance.</note> and presented him with several questions regarding <term>natural magic<note>A branch of philosophy that sought to understand the hidden "occult" powers of the natural world (like magnetism or medicinal herbs) through observation rather than demonic intervention.</note></term> and alchemy. *Erasmus* candidly declared that he considered magic to be nothing more than empty vapor or idle words; he noted that while alchemy did not seem quite as baseless as the <term>Kabbalah<note>A form of Jewish mysticism. Renaissance thinkers like Agrippa attempted to integrate it into Christian philosophy, though it was often viewed with suspicion by the Church.</note></term>, there were so many approaches to alchemy that it was infinitely difficult to find the right one. 

Since the traveler found no satisfaction with *Erasmus*, he asked him at least for a letter of recommendation to *Agrippa*. With this in hand, after a journey of more than two hundred miles, he finally arrived in Brussels. "Would to God," he wrote in the note announcing his arrival, "that I might find grace in the eyes of my lord and master, and could serve him for a time without any reward, as a servant or assistant, to learn heavenly wisdom and finally cast off the mask of ignorance with which I have hitherto been covered! I know not what holds me back from following in your footsteps and kissing those very footsteps." 

*Agrippa* received the priest, named Andreas, kindly and kept him with him for several days, though in such a short time it was impossible to impart much new and hidden wisdom to the stranger. *Agrippa* assured *Erasmus* that, despite the frankness with which he had written his *Declamation on the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>Agrippa’s most famous work, *De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum et artium*, which attacked the pretensions of all human knowledge.</note>, in all matters of faith he thought no differently than the Holy Catholic Church *).

He argued that the Emperor was a human being like any other, and could be led astray by his passions or by "cunning rascals" just like anyone else **). The Emperor, he claimed, was confusing suspicion or doubt with proven guilt; this confusion could not prevent *Agrippa* from defending his innocence. The articles from Louvain written against Agrippa were even more wretchedly composed and conceived than those of the Cologne theologians against Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin (1455–1522) was a German humanist whose defense of Hebrew books led to a landmark legal battle with the conservative theologians of Cologne; this was a defining conflict between humanism and scholasticism.</note> <margin>Works of Agrippa, Vol. II, pages 264–272.</margin>. They accused Agrippa of things that he had not asserted in earnest, or at least not unconditionally <margin>For example: That the devil was the inventor of the monk's cowl; that all sciences are harmful, or that the best thing is to know nothing.</margin>; or things which Augustine or the Holy Scripture had taught in plain words <margin>For example: That soldiers and merchants rarely achieve true repentance; that the Holy Scripture is sufficient unto itself, and so forth.</margin>; or things which were incontrovertibly proven by history and experience <margin>For example: That even the prophets, evangelists, apostles, and other saints erred in some matters; that the veneration of saints is mixed with idolatry; that only ecclesiastical law forbids the marriage of priests, and so forth. Since I, says Agrippa, have called my writing itself a <term>declamation<note>In the Renaissance, a "declamation" was a rhetorical exercise where an author argued a specific position to demonstrate oratorical skill or provoke thought, often without it being their personal, "serious" belief.</note></term>, it proves just as much ignorance as a desire for slander that the Louvain article-writers take everything defended therein as my own serious opinion <gloss>assertions</gloss> <margin>Collected Works, Vol. II, pages 273, 326.</margin>. A declamation does not judge, does not decide; rather, it says this in jest and that in earnest. At times it speaks in the mind of its author, at times in the soul of others. <meta>This page continues Agrippa’s defense against the Louvain theologians. I do not [condemn] all arts and sciences here, but I merely declaim upon their vanity and uncertainty, and I rebuke those who neglect the Word of God and place their entire confidence in worldly sciences, where they are forever learning and disputing without ever arriving at the knowledge of the truth. I demonstrate which heresies and errors have arisen and continue to arise from worldly sciences when they are not ordered according to the Word of God, through which alone one can distinguish the true from the false, the good from the evil, and without which all learning is vain.

But even supposing that I had erred here and there, would it then be Christian to put the worst possible construction upon my assertions, and to forgive nothing regardless of my other merits? How much does one encounter in the writings of Saint Jerome and Augustine, of Tertullian and Lactantius—and even more in those of Saint Thomas, Scotus, Ockham <note>The original text uses "Vocam," likely a transcription error or variant for William of Ockham, a major 14th-century Scholastic philosopher.</note>, and other lights of the schools—which sounds dangerous and heretical? How has the veneration of many images of saints not been exaggerated? People compete with one another to decorate them like market stalls with more or larger ornaments, and to hang them with purchased indulgences or fabricated miracle stories, just to make one appear more divine and more miracle-working than the other. 

How often have we seen that during good wine harvests, the image of Saint Urban—just like the statue of Bacchus in former times—is crowned with vine leaves and carried through the streets of cities and villages to the sound of noisy music, accompanied by a priest? In my opinion, therefore, in our times nothing is better than to know nothing; nothing is safer than to write nothing, because one cannot make anything public without offending many. I have not written to the Regent for the reason that I hope my outstanding salary will be paid, but only to heap even more coals of fire upon the heads of my enemies <note>A biblical reference to Romans 12:20, meaning to repay unkindness with kindness to make the adversary feel shame, though Agrippa uses it here with a more vengeful tone.</note>, and to gain all the more reason and material for the most emphatic revenge. The letter to the Regent of the Netherlands was likewise composed in Latin, and Agrippa asked Rhreytter to ensure, if possible, that the Princess read this letter herself, rather than having it read and summarized for her by others. One sees from this example, as from Agrippa's earlier letters to the Queen Mother in France and to the Regent Margaret, that in the first half of the sixteenth century, the most prominent daughters of princes were, as a rule, instructed in the Latin language.

Agrippa first recounts to Queen Mary <note>Mary of Hungary (1505–1558), who became Governor of the Netherlands in 1531.</note> how great the merits of himself and his ancestors were toward the House of Austria; with what dangers and sacrifices he had left France to come to the Burgundian court; how the Emperor had allowed himself to be turned against him and his book *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "de vanitate scientiarum"</note> by certain crafty hypocrites, and would likely have ruined him had the monarch's mind not been somewhat appeased by Cardinal Campeggio and by the Cardinal-Bishop of Liège <note>Erard de La Marck.</note>: how the Burgundian financiers had first stalled him regarding the determination of his salary, and then set a sum—

—not at all commensurate with his merits, and were now withholding even this meager salary (with which he had pacified his creditors in Mechelen) under the pretext that he was not in the country and was not performing his office. He argued that the office of historian and archivist did not tie him to a specific location. His predecessor had constantly made journeys through Italy, France, and other countries. Even while absent, he fulfilled his duties, having drafted the history of the war which the Duke of Bourbon <note>Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, who led imperial troops against France.</note> had waged for the Emperor in Italy, and having collected with great effort all documents and reports concerning the Emperor’s expedition against the Turks. In addition to these works, he had undertaken a much more difficult task, and one more important for the honor of the House of Austria: the defense of the Queen of England <note>Catherine of Aragon, whose marriage to Henry VIII was being annulled. Agrippa wrote in her defense, supporting the validity of her marriage.</note>. If he were denied his rights, he lacked neither the means nor the will to avenge insults which in former times had been repaid with fire, sword, and poison. However, he maintained too high an opinion of the Queen to expect such treatment from her fairness and wisdom.

That the love for mysterious books and secret sciences, as well as for secret societies, accompanied Agrippa until the end of his life is evident from a letter he received from a learned friend in the service of Cardinal Campeggio at the beginning of the year 1533. This initiated confidant sought out Cabbalistic writings for Agrippa in all the cities of Italy, and reported to him that he had spoken with Georgius Venetus <note>Francesco Giorgio (1460–1541), a Venetian Franciscan friar and author of *De Harmonia Mundi*, known for his Christian Kabbalah.</note> about Agrippa, as well as about their shared studies and secrets, and...

Just as Hoogstraten <note>Jacob van Hoogstraten, a Dominican inquisitor and a fierce opponent of the Reformation and humanist scholars.</note> had laid claim against Agrippa’s book *On the Vanity of the Sciences*, so too did Conrad Rollin of Ulm—a second primary figure in the conflict between the Cologne theologians and Reuchlin <note>Johannes Reuchlin was a pioneer of Hebrew studies whose work was attacked by the Inquisition in a famous legal battle.</note>—rise up against the books *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "de occulta philosophia"</note>, which had begun to be printed at the start of the year 1533. He accused the monks themselves of being the primary authors of the decline of the university, and called upon the Senate to suppress the tyranny of these destructive men and protect Agrippa against their chicanery. Agrippa addresses the most hateful accusations in the preface of his work—which he foresaw would be made against him—with great cleverness. Already the title, he says, will set many of my enviers and enemies up in arms, and provoke them to the outcry that I, as a **magician** <note>original: "Magier"</note>, teach forbidden arts, scatter the seeds of heresy, offend pious ears, and am a scandal to pious souls. It will be of no help if I call out to these screamers that the word "magician" <note>original: "Magier"</note> does not mean a sorcerer, but a wise man, a priest, a prophet: that the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses who were believed by Renaissance humanists to have predicted the coming of Christ.</note> were "magicians" and nevertheless prophesied Christ: that the Wise Men of the East, through their secret miraculous arts, recognized Christ and were the first to come,

First, following the third book, are two letters from Agrippa to the Father of Aquapendente, then a letter of the same to a "friend in the royal court" <note>original: "Amicum in aula regia"</note>; and this letter is the twenty-sixth in the fifth book of the complete collection of letters, where it is listed not as a letter by Agrippa, but as one from a friend to Agrippa. Finally follow the chapters from the book *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>original: "de vanitate scientiarum"</note> regarding magic, Kabbalah, etc., and indeed under the title: *H. C. Agrippa’s censure or retraction concerning magic, from his declamation on the vanity of the sciences and the excellence of the word of God* <note>original: "H. C. Agrippae censura sive retractatio de magia, ex sua declamatione de vanitate scientiarum, et excellentia verbi Dei"</note>. Agrippa most likely had all these pieces printed so that he could tell his enemies that he had long ago revoked a large part of the content of the books on secret wisdom: that he has always loathed all connections with evil spirits and the "black art": that he has always placed genuine magic in a perfect knowledge of and union with the Deity: and that he had the work *On Occult Philosophy* printed primarily to prevent an incorrect or falsified printing.

to worship Him: that finally the name "Magic" is pleasing to philosophers and theologians and is not even foreign to the Gospel. But perverse spirits and hearts will sooner give up all philosophy, theology, and perhaps even the Gospel itself, before they will allow the word "Magic" to be considered unobjectionable. To these I now advise that they do not read my books; for to them, they are poisonous: they could break their heads, or even lead them to the very gates of hell. You favorable ones, however, who read just as bees collect honey, step forward: you will certainly draw a great deal of pleasure and no small benefit from my work. Even in the books of physicians, you find prescriptions for poisons themselves alongside the prescriptions for healing medicines and antidotes. I confess, moreover, that magic teaches many unnecessary things that merely excite wonder. These too you can leave unused, and yet make yourselves familiar with the causes of them. Who, however, would not find those parts of magic not merely useful, but also necessary, which—without the slightest harm to religion and without offense to the Divine Majesty—provide instruction on how one can remove diseases and other evils, destroy incantations and sorceries, and preserve or prolong one's life, fortune, and honor? I repeat the reminder that I have written much more as a narrator than as an advocate. Trusting in this warning, I was able to touch upon many things that I otherwise would have had to pass over. Agrippa divides his work on hidden wisdom into three books according to the number of worlds: namely, the physical or elemental world, the celestial world, and the intellectual or intelligible world; of which one deals with natural magic, the second with celestial magic, and the third with religious or ceremonial magic.

The substance of all earthly things, says Agrippa, consists of the four elements <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire, the fundamental building blocks of matter in pre-modern science.</note> *), without the knowledge of which no magus <note>A practitioner of magic; a wise man or philosopher-scientist.</note> can accomplish anything **). <meta>This page continues the summary and analysis of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa’s "Three Books of Occult Philosophy." It transitions from his defense of the work to explaining specific claims within the first book, focusing on "natural magic" and the theoretical mechanics of how hidden forces work in the universe.</meta>

It is possible, without superstition and without the cooperation of spirits, for one person to communicate their thoughts to another even across the greatest distance. The exact time required for this cannot be precisely determined, but there is no doubt that it must occur within twenty-four hours. I myself can do this, and have done so often. Even Abbot Tritheim <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a celebrated monk, polymath, and cryptic writer who was Agrippa’s mentor.</note> was familiar with this secret. By means of certain mirrors, images of all kinds of things can be produced in the air, which the ignorant mistake for spirits or the souls of the departed. An even more wondrous feat is that by which certain images, or written letters, are held up to the rays of the full moon on a clear night until they are reflected on the moon’s disk in such a way that another person, who has been instructed in the method, can see and read everything in the moon. This secret, which is particularly important in besieged cities, was formerly practiced by Pythagoras; and it is still not unknown to several living persons today, including myself.

All types of things composed of elements follow the nature of those elements—even the senses and passions of men—so that they always have a greater affinity for one element than for the others *). The qualities and powers of natural bodies are of three types. Some arise from the elements themselves, such as heating and cooling, etc. Others arise from the mixture of the elements, such as digestive, dissolving, or strengthening powers, etc. And still others finally act upon specific parts of the body, such as those that stimulate milk or urine, etc.

*) Book I, chapter 7.

<column-break/>

Distinguished from all these qualities and powers are the so-called "hidden" or "occult" properties <term>occult properties: powers in nature that have no obvious physical explanation, like magnetism</term>, the causes of which no human understanding can fathom. To this category belong the powers of many things to repel poison, to attract iron, and so forth. These hidden properties can produce great effects even when contained in small quantities, which is not the case with elementary properties <note>Agrippa argues that while you need a lot of fire to get a lot of heat, a tiny amount of a "hidden" substance can have a massive effect.</note>. The hidden properties are infused into the things of this lower world by God through the World Soul <note>original: "Weltseele" or *Anima Mundi*</note>, and through the harmonious cooperation of celestial spirits and the influences and aspects of the stars *). The self-moving spirit and the inherently inert or immovable body cannot be joined together except through a certain intermediary being <note>original: "Mittelwesen"</note> that is, as it were, soul but not body, or non-soul and yet already body; and this is the World Spirit <note>original: "Weltgeist" or *Spiritus Mundi*</note>, which is also called the fifth element or quintessence †). Just as the powers of our own soul act through the spirit residing within us in all parts of the human body, so too the powers of the World Soul spread across all things in the entire universe by means of the World Spirit. For nothing exists which has not received a ray of the World Soul and its power. However, it communicates itself most strongly to those things which have drawn most from the World Spirit; this World Spirit is in turn drawn down through the rays of the stars, provided that earthly things make themselves fit to receive them. The World Spirit is most useful when one understands how to separate it from the other elements, or how to use those things in which it is especially concentrated.

†) Ibid. chapter 14.

Stones and metals have similarities with plants; plants with animals; animals with the heavens and celestial bodies; celestial bodies with the heavenly intelligences; and these, finally, with the divine attributes and with God himself. All lower beings are so precisely connected with the higher ones that the influence of the latter descends to the very lowest like a stretched string; and, if only one of these is touched, the entire chain of beings trembles and resonates in the same way as the strings of a well-tuned lyre †).

Because of this interconnectedness of all beings, there are certainly natural bodies through which the dead can be awakened, good and evil spirits summoned, and other wonderful effects produced *). This also includes the binding of people (*ligatio* <note>original: "ligatio"; the magical practice of "binding" a person's actions or feelings</note>) toward hate and love, health and sickness; the binding of thieves so that they cannot steal, and of merchants so that they cannot trade; the binding of armies, ships, mills, streams, fields, lightning bolts, fires, dogs, birds, and wild game. Words are signs of things; and as such, they receive wonderful powers partly from the objects they represent, and partly from the one who made them signs of things **). Especially the <term>proper names</term> <note>original: "Nomina Propria"</note>, or the designations of individual objects, contain the properties of the things which are indicated by them. ### Effectiveness and Properties

**Unity** is the **principle** <note>original: "Principium"; the fundamental source or origin</note> of all things. It alone is everything, and outside of it, there is nothing. Everything has sprung from One, and everything that strives to return to this One must first cast off its multiplicity. There is only one God, one world, one sun, one phoenix, one queen bee, one leader and guardian of flocks, one ruling limb on the human body, one all-conquering and all-penetrating element, one wonderful **subject** <note>here referring to a fundamental substance or essence</note> that is found in heaven and on earth, in animals, plants, minerals, and everywhere else—yet is known by few, and without which neither **alchemy** nor **natural magic** can reach its goal \*). In this manner, *Agrippa* explains the properties of all numbers up to twelve, and throughout he adds a **Scale** <note>original: "Scala"; a hierarchical ladder or table of correspondences</note> in which the primary objects are specified that correspond to each number in the **archetypal world** <note>original: "mundo archetypo"; the realm of pure ideas or the divine mind</note>, in the intellectual, the celestial, the elemental world, in the small world (or man), and finally in the underworld \*\*). From here, he proceeds to the symbols of numbers; to the signs which are unique and sacred to each star and part of the heavens; to the doctrine of the **harmony of the spheres** <note>the ancient theory that the movements of celestial bodies create a divine form of music</note>, and the wonderful powers of tones and harmonies, as well as the harmony of the human body and the human soul †). He concludes these investigations with thoughts on the effects of the heavens and the celestial bodies, their signs, omens, images, and souls ††). The world, the heavens,

<page-num>377</page-num>

the stars, and the elements themselves, it is said in the 56th chapter, have **souls**, and besides these, they have spirits through which the souls are connected to the bodies. Since the smallest and most contemptible little animals have souls, it would be absurd to believe that the world, the heavens, the stars, and elements—which give life and sensation to all other things—should have no souls. Just as the heavenly souls act down upon this underworld through the heavenly bodies, so a wise **magician** <note>original: "Magus"</note> can, in turn, act upward to the heavenly intelligences through sacred and mysterious words and prayers; not as if these beings "heard" the words and prayers as we do, but because, by virtue of the exact connection of the entire world, the higher things are moved by the lower. Effects of this kind are no more "above" or "against" nature than the enchantments that a skilled musician produces in the souls of his listeners through the power of his tones. The most powerful prayers are those directed to the first Creator of all things; and this consideration paves the way for *Agrippa* to transition to the third book, in which he deals with religious or **Ceremonial Magic**.

The knowledge of divine things, says *Agrippa* \*), purifies our spirit of errors, makes it divine, gives all our operations an infallible outcome, protects us against all the arts of evil spirits, and subjects them to us; likewise, it makes the good angels and all the powers of nature our servants by drawing us up to the highest Primal Being. As I have mentioned elsewhere, this work transforms the whole world into a magic garden. All laws of nature are instantly suspended or reversed. Every being is a center point or a tool for wonderful powers and effects. The underworld is shaped entirely by the influences of the heavens and celestial bodies; and all celestial bodies and spirits must, in turn, obey the magician and conjurer. Regardless of this, Agrippa’s work received the greatest applause from most of the most famous scholars in all parts of Europe; and this alone shows how meager the beginnings of true enlightenment, or the genuine knowledge of nature and man, still were at that time.

Proud of the victory he had won over the monks of Cologne through the publication of the books *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: *de occulta philosophia*</note>, and full of confidence in the favor of the Prince <note>Hermann von Wied, the Prince-Elector of Cologne</note> who had secured this victory for him, Agrippa resolved from then on to wage an eternal war with all monks. He believed their anger was eternal and irreconcilable, and their revenge all the more dangerous the more one yielded to them or appeared to fear them †). Erasmus advised him against this plan and urged him to devote the time he intended for this dangerous struggle to the advancement of useful knowledge.

Agrippa remained in Cologne until the year 1535, despite having received enticing invitations to Italy <note>Agrippa often struggled to find a permanent home due to his controversial reputation and frequent falling out with patrons.</note> two years earlier from a friend he could trust \*). During the final year of his stay in Bonn, he separated from his third wife, who was a native of Mechelen; we know only this of her: that she was cast out by her husband \*\*). The resentment or the shame regarding this separation was perhaps the primary cause of the isolation in which Agrippa eventually lived in Bonn. This seclusion gradually took such a hold on him, or became such a habit, that he often did not leave his study for eight days at a time †). Perhaps his domestic misfortune also drove him to leave Bonn in 1535 to visit his friends in Lyon once more ††). However, on the journey to Lyon, Agrippa was taken prisoner by order of Francis I, because he had written unfavorable things about the Queen Mother <note>Louise of Savoy, with whom Agrippa had a famously contentious relationship after serving as her physician.</note>. Although his friends eventually secured his release from custody, he died in Grenoble a few months after his liberation. Around this time, his faithful student, Johann Wier <note>Johann Wier, or Weyer, later became a famous physician known for his early opposition to the witch trials.</note>, was residing in Paris †††).

He was a strange mixture of high enlightenment and the most contemptible superstition, possessing a captivating oral eloquence and a continuous inclination toward supernatural sciences, interrupted only by brief intervals of resentment and doubt. His Latin writing style was sometimes gritty, sometimes rich and florid, yet neither pure nor correct \*).

The acquired perfections of his spirit deserve to be admired in **Agrippa** more than in others, when one considers the adverse fates and consuming worries with which he had to struggle for the greatest part of his life. Agrippa devoted much less care to the formation of his character than to the cultivation of his mind. He retained all the faults of his temperament until his death, and repeatedly committed the same missteps, no matter how often he had been warned or how harshly he had been punished for them. He never ceased to be irrationally irascible, and in this sudden anger, to vent the most irrational threats, insults, and boasts. No less inextinguishable were his restlessness, which hunted him from place to place and from one situation to another; his entirely inexcusable versatility and duplicity; and finally, the resulting deception—worthy only of a common adventurer and a quack—with which he pretended to understand, teach, or practice things of which he himself must have known he did not understand, and could not teach or practice. The best, or brightest side of his character is his natural inclination and capacity for domestic happiness, and for the joys of friendship and sociability. It was a great deal for an adventurer leading such a wandering life as Agrippa that he could resolve to marry,

It was even more significant that the otherwise so unstable Agrippa, despite the previous embarrassment into which the support of a wife, children, and servants plunged him, loved his first two wives faithfully and tenderly until their deaths; and that this otherwise so unruly man never offended his worthy wives with an outbreak of wildness that was not already calmed before the rising of the sun. Agrippa loved his friends, if perhaps not as fervently as his wives, at least just as faithfully and steadfastly; and this love for his friends was repaid by an equally unchangeable mutual affection. Everywhere Agrippa lived for a time—in Cologne, Metz, Geneva, Lyon, Paris, in Italy, and in Switzerland—he gained friends who remained devoted to him with the sincerest love throughout his life. Even if a penchant for the secret arts <note>Likely referring to occultism, alchemy, and the Kabbalah, which Agrippa famously studied.</note> was for many the first spark of their affection, and later one of the bonds of their friendship toward Agrippa, such friendship would not have become so unshakable as it remained with everyone if Agrippa's heart had not been worthy of the love of wise and good men. Agrippa was just as kind and helpful a master and teacher as he was a loving husband and friend. <term>Johann Wier</term> <note>Agrippa's most famous student, who later became a physician and critic of witch trials.</note>, who for several years was his <term>Amanuensis</term> <note>A personal assistant or secretary who transcribed dictated text.</note> or house-friend, calls him in several places his venerable master and teacher *), with whom he always lived in

Among these, he loved Monsieur so "childishly"—as even his student **Wier** <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who later became a famous critic of witch hunts.</note> testifies <note>original Latin: "Quod canem hunc pueriliter nimis amaret."</note>—that he not only had the dog constantly at his feet while working and at his side while eating, but also in his bed at night. He often kissed the dog as if it were a lover or a child. From this excessive love for his dog Monsieur, a legend arose: that Agrippa constantly carried the Devil with him in the form of a dog, and that this dog later vanished all at once. This popular superstition was further strengthened by the fact that Agrippa—who often did not go out or see anyone for a week—nevertheless knew all the important news from across Europe, because he received daily letters from his learned friends in all various regions <note>Johann Weyer, the same source cited above.</note>. Johann Wier did not hold it against the "great crowd" of his contemporaries for suspecting such things of Agrippa. However, he was rightly astonished that famous and learned men, such as **Jovius** <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician and historian.</note> and others, could believe these absurd fairy tales and repeat them in their own writings <note>original Latin footnote: "I cannot sufficiently wonder here that men of such great reputation sometimes speak, feel, and write so foolishly based on the emptiest rumors of the common folk." <meta>This page continues the assessment of Agrippa's reputation, transitioning from his personal habits and pets to his historical legacy as a scholar who was simultaneously a critic of the church and a prominent promoter of the occult.</meta>

It is among the characteristic differences between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and then the latter half of the eighteenth century <note>The author is highlighting the shift from the Renaissance/Reformation era to the Enlightenment, when belief in literal magic began to fade among the educated elite.</note>, that well-known writers could accuse other scholars of sorcery <term>sorcery: "Zauberey" in the original; the practice of magic, often implying a pact with the devil</term> without making themselves look ridiculous, whereas today one would be mocked for even bothering to refute such nonsense. As long as it was still believed that someone could carry the devil around with them in the form of a dog <note>This refers to the legend that Agrippa’s black dog, "Monsieur," was actually a familiar spirit or the devil in disguise.</note>, no one gave more cause for the legend of such a spirit—and for the suspicion of magic in general—than Agrippa did through his life and his writings.

The harm, as well as the benefit, which Agrippa produced as a teacher and author can no more be precisely determined than the literary merits or faults of other scholars. However, as far as we humans are able to generally state the effects of individuals from distant centuries on their contemporaries, one cannot help but believe that Agrippa did more harm than good as a teacher and writer. The abuses and errors which he criticized <note>Agrippa was a fierce critic of corruption within the Catholic Church and the legal profession of his time.</note> had long been rebuked by others, even if not as boldly and strongly as by him. Indeed, the very violence with which he attacked various parties often proved more detrimental than beneficial to the good cause. On the other hand, throughout his entire life, Agrippa contributed greatly to the spread of supposedly supernatural arts—or all kinds of superstition—through his teachings and writings. The secret society which he established and propagated through France, Italy, England, and Germany was

<column-break/>

the first of its kind to be founded by a famous scholar; and it was undoubtedly the mother or the model for all others that emerged in the following times.

I conclude the life of Agrippa with a short history and chronology of his writings, which can be divided into those that are printed, those written but not printed, and finally those that were indeed planned, but of which it is uncertain whether they were ever actually written or completed. The printed writings are further distinguished by whether we know when they were written and printed, only when they were written but not printed, or neither when they were written nor when they were first printed.

### I.
## Agrippa’s Printed Writings.

The first among his writings were his *Declamation on the Excellence of the Female Sex* <note>original: "declamatio de excellentia sexus fœminini"</note>, which he wrote in 1509 in Dole, and the *Expostulation against Catilinetus* <note>original: "expostulatio contra Catilinetum"</note>, which he wrote in 1510 in London. These were followed by the books *On Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "de occulta philosophia"</note>, which he composed shortly thereafter *). After he had sent this youthful work to Abbot Tritheim <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous Benedictine abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and magic.</note> for review before his journey to Italy, and had received it back with the highest praise, he expanded it or wrote *commentaries* <term>commentaries: explanatory notes or supplementary essays meant to clarify a primary text</term> upon it, which he lost for a time during or after the battle in which Francis I defeated the Swiss †). The first draft of the magical work, which he had delivered to Abbot Tritheim, circulated as a manuscript in all the countries of Europe for many years. It was only after Agrippa’s return from France that he reworked the books *On Occult Philosophy* in Antwerp so extensively that he now recognized them as a work of his more mature years. In the imperial privilege <note>A 16th-century form of copyright or legal protection granted by the Emperor to an author or printer.</note> which he received in 1529 for several of his writings, the books *On Occult Philosophy* are mentioned by name. The first book was printed in 1531—

The Imperial Privilege of 1529 gave Agrippa the exclusive right to have his *Commentaries on the Brief Art of Lull* and the *Abbreviated Table of the Commentaries on the Brief Art of Lull* <note>original: "Commentaria in artem brevem Lullii" and "Tabula abbreviata Commentariorum in artem brevem Lullii"</note> <note>Oper. From the dedications, I suspect that Agrippa wrote the commentaries himself during his stay in Italy, and the tables for these commentaries during his stay in Cologne after he had left Metz. From this, one can see that the <term>Lullian Art</term> <note>A system created by the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull, using logical combinations of symbols to discover and prove truths across all fields of knowledge.</note> was at that time counted among the secret arts and was valued in all parts of Europe, even by famous men. Because you, **Agrippa** writes to his patron, devote yourself with such diligence to the hidden sciences, I will satisfy your desire and also admit you to the inner secrets. I am therefore not presenting you with a common or well-known art, but with the Queen of all arts, under whose guidance you can easily learn all other arts and sciences and attain an extraordinary level of scholarship. This Queen of all arts is the Art of Invention by **Raimund Lullus**, which is of such excellence, universality, and certainty that through it alone—without effort or outside help—one can find the truth about all subjects of human knowledge, unfailingly and with the greatest reliability. Furthermore, it encompasses all other sciences, resolves all doubts and difficulties across every branch of our knowledge, provides proofs that no one is able to contradict, and does not require the help of other sciences at all; rather, it alone organizes and gives stability and certainty to the other sciences, even to the Holy Scripture. It possesses universal and irrefutable methods of proof and principles, in which the principles and methods of the other sciences are contained, like the particular within the general. This same Art of Invention is so easy that by means of it, even children can speak with proper expertise in almost all sciences; and many old men, who previously never occupied themselves with the sciences, became very learned men in just a few months. The Lullian Art thus alone compensates for the lack and the con-

straints of time. So that this does not seem like a fable, one need only name two men famous throughout all Italy from our own age: **Petrus Daguinus Mediatus** <note>Pedro Daguí, a 15th-century Majorcan scholar and follower of Llull.</note> and **Jacob Januarius** <note>Jacopo Gennaro.</note>. The first of these two men had, in his thirty-seventh year, hardly learned the first elements of the sciences when he began to apply himself to the Lullian Art for seven months; he was then suddenly gazed upon as a wonder by all the scholars in Italy. All of Italy has heard him speak with admiration, and his writings also stand as monuments to his great scholarship. But it is even more wonderful that **Jacob Januarius**, who until his thirty-fifth year had not concerned himself with scholarship at all, progressed so far through the Lullian Art alone that, as his works prove, he was second to none of his learned contemporaries. It is well known that the Spaniard **Ferdinand von Cordova** <note>Fernando de Córdoba, a renowned polymath and child prodigy.</note> earned the greatest fame through this art at all the high schools <note>A term for universities.</note> on both sides of the Alps; and also **Raymund von Sebonde** <note>Ramon Sibiuda, author of "Natural Theology."</note>, the author of a natural theology, shows sufficiently through his writings how far he advanced in this art. Dedicated to this same Raymund are **Jacob Faber** <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a prominent French humanist.</note> and **Carl Boville** <note>Charles de Bovelles, a French philosopher and mathematician.</note> of Paris, men of universally esteemed merit. ## III.
### Agrippa’s Writings,
->which he intended to produce, but for which it is uncertain whether he completed them: Also regarding suspicious writings, and the editions of all his printed works.<-

In 1526, *Agrippa* had the intention of writing a book *On Political Nobility* <note>original: "de nobilitate politica"</note> \*), which, however, he does not mention again in the future. In the year 1532, he informed Queen *Mary* <note>Mary of Hungary, Governor of the Netherlands</note> that he had made a draft of the history of the Italian war which the Duke of *Bourbon* had waged against *Francis I*; that he had collected all the documents necessary for the history of *Charles V’s* undertaking against the Barbary <note>referring to the North African states</note> coast, and that he wished to write a defense of the Queen of England <note>Catherine of Aragon, during the period of her divorce from Henry VIII</note> \*\*). Shortly thereafter, in a letter to the Council of Cologne, he mentions his book *On the Crimes and Heresies of the Preaching Friars* <note>original: "de fratrum prædicatorum sceleribus et hæresibus," referring to the Dominican Order</note> in such an ambiguous way that one might believe he had actually completed its preparation †). Already in the year 1526, he mentioned his own <term>Geomancy: a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</term>—which was entirely different from the common variety—as a writing he had composed some time ago but had lost, he knew not how \*). He does not state in any of his later letters that the lost *Geomancy* was ever found again. I therefore doubt all the more that the *Lecture on the Discipline of Geomancy* <note>original: "lectura in Geomanticam disciplinam"</note>, which is found among Agrippa’s works \*\*), is authentic, as this lecture is composed exactly in the manner that Agrippa describes the common geomancy <note>Agrippa was often critical of "common" superstitious practices, even while writing about the occult</note>.

Our library possesses three different editions of Agrippa’s collected works. The first consists of two volumes and was printed in Lyon in 1550 by the brothers Godefridus and Marcellus Beringus <note>original: "apud Godefridum et Marcellum Beringos, fratres"</note>. The first volume bears only the title: *Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim’s Three Books on Occult Philosophy* <note>original: "Henrici Cornelii Agrippæ ab Nettesheym - - - de occulta philosophia libri III"</note>. This first volume contains neither the spurious fourth book of *Occult Philosophy*, nor the *Geomancy*, nor other genuine or non-genuine magical writings which were later printed together with Agrippa’s works. The second volume contains the letters, speeches, and other writings of Agrippa, and has the title: *The Latter Part of the Works of H. C. Agrippa* <note>original: "H. C. Agrippæ - - - operum pars posterior"</note>. Among the two remaining editions in our library, one bears the date 1600, while the second has no date at all. On both, it is written: *At the Bering brothers, Lyon* <note>original: "Lugduni apud Beringos fratres"</note>. Despite this, I consider both editions to be reprints <note>In this context, the author implies they are likely unauthorized or pirated editions</note> which

were printed neither in Lyon nor by the Bering brothers. The printing and paper are of much poorer quality than in the original edition. Both have different and entirely distinct title woodcuts compared to the first edition of 1550. Both lack the index of the latter, and I also believe that the negligence of the pirate-publishers is the cause of the many printing errors in the 1600 edition and the one without a stated place of publication. So that it might not seem suspicious that the two Bering brothers, who had arranged the first edition in 1550, were still undertaking a new edition in the year 1600, the first names of the original publishers were omitted, and simply *at the Bering brothers* <note>original: "apud Beringos fratres"</note> was placed on the title. Furthermore, the two later editions correspond with one another most exactly. 

The first pirate-publisher sought to distinguish himself by including the fourth book of *Occult Philosophy* (of which it is stated, however, *as it is thought to be spurious* <note>original: "ut putatur spurius"</note>), the substituted *Geomancy*, and a multitude of magical writings by Peter de Abano, Tritheim, Gerard of Cremona, Arbatel, and others. Perhaps the publisher of the 1600 edition (of which the undated one is yet another reprint) was not even the first pirate-publisher. On the title of the 1600 edition, it says: *to which, besides all the tables, has been newly added the Notary Art, which you find placed in its proper location* <note>original: "quibus præter omnes tabulas noviter accessit Ars notaria, quam suo loco interpositam invenis"</note>. From this, one must conclude that after the original edition, another had appeared in which the fourth book of *Occult Philosophy* and all the other pieces provided by the 1600 reprint were contained—except for the <term>Ars Notaria: a medieval system of ritual magic intended to grant the practitioner rapid mastery of the liberal arts and memory</term>. Otherwise, the title of the 1600 edition would have noted not just the *Ars Notaria*, but also the other newly added articles. The reprint without the name of the...
